maintopic: INSURANCE ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext:
Mr. W. H. BENNETT (East Simcoe) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 45,
. to amend the Insurance Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this Bill is almost in the same terms as that introduced by the late Mr. Lancaster a few years ago and in view of the fact that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) has a notice on -the paper for the introduction of a Bill to amend the Insurance Act, I would ask that this also be allowed to go to the same committee and perhaps the two could be taken up together. This amendment which I ask leave to introduce has reference to companies upon the backs of whose certificates were endorsed certain terms as to the payment, and the rate of payment, of the premiums. It is alleged that one company, which I need not name, have, by arbitrary action, gone outside of the terms and conditions which they have at times made with insurers and it is to place these persons who have been insured in a fair position that this amendment is introduced. The discussion of this matter will be of considerable length and I would ask that it be postponed until the bill is before the committee.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: BANK ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext:
Mr. L. A. LAPOINTE (Montreal, St. James) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 46, to amend the Bank Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to detain the House just now with any lengthy explanation of the question which underlies the principle of the Bill I desire to introduce, in amendment to the Bank Act. An opportunity for the discussion of this question will occur later on. I may say that this is a most important question to the public at large and I believe there are hundreds of thousands of people in Canada who will be grateful for such legislation. The purport of the measure is to have the rate of interest fixed by statute on saving bank deposits at not less than four per cent. The amendment would read as follows:
Section 92 of the Ban'-: Act, chapter 9 of the Statutes of 1913 is amended by striking out
the word "whatever" in the first line of said section and inserting in lieu thereof "not less than four per cent".
My intention is to have an understanding with my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) on the subject of this Bill before its second reading.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext:
["Mr. Speaker, from the remarks by the eloquent orators who have hereto taken part in the debate on the Budget, I took it that the main question was that of free wheat. The subect is not wanting in interest. It may be considered from two viewpoints, as to-day's discussion shows.
The enhanced price of wheat in the western provinces must necessarily produce an increase in the cost of flour, and so the people in the East must pay a much higher price for this staple commodity. Mr. Speaker, I heard the hon. member for As-siniboia (Mr. Turriff) censuring strongly the Government. At every session he was heard in condemnation of the Government because the latter would not grant to the western provinces a greater measure of reciprocity. Yet the gentleman hails from .an eastern constituency, having been bom, as myse'lf, in the county of Rimouski, where he has still important interests and many relatives.
I think he must remember-having been brought up in that section of my province- that the province of Quebec has some interests it seeks to protect, and he cannot but admit that the western part of Canada
should not monopolize all our attention and efforts.
In support of my claim, I shall quote from *a speech I delivered last year in this House. I shall read the English version, so as to be understood by the hon. members who -do not understand French. My remarks were as follows:-
All the points of the question have been sifted again and again and all its aspects scrutinized, and from all the twaddle what stands out clear to me is that the western members are using the question as an electoral war-horse. They take it up as a good means of boosting their case and ensuring their reelection.
A while ago one of the western members attacked the Government for not giving the farmers all the help they were entitled to. Yet, if any people should grumble against want of solicitude on the part of the Government, surely not those farmers. Every time they are the victims of some slight mishap, a drought or a frost, they appeal to the Government and immediately millions of dollars are put at their disposal to enable them to tide over the crisis. Our eastern farmers have not the same recourse. If the harvest is bad, or they suffer from frost, they have to shift for themselves without any one coming to their aid. Of ail farmers who have no reason to grumble, those of the prairies are first, for the Government is lavish in its favours to them.
The same orator complains that agricultural implements were not allowed to be imported free of duty from the United States, he claims the tariff in that respect is detrimental to them, and in support of his contention he maintains that the higher price paid for the same machinery in Canada than obtains across the border is disadvantageous to the farmer, that it is in fact money taken from the purse of the farmer and given to the manufacturer. So be it, but, in my opinion, when the hon. member further stated that only the manufacturers reap the benefit of the tariff, he is clearly mistaken. The workmen also find) it he to their benefit. It must not be forgotten that in those manufactories are to he found workmen to whom the tariff is a benefit in the form of employment. Granted even that an article he something higher in price in Canada than it is in the United States, it seems to me that if the western people were good patriots, they would' not begrudge this slight sacrifice to allow Canadian workmen to find his sustenance in this, our common country. After all we are not an agglomeration of two or three Canadas, but we form an entity destined to live as a whole in this country, and no section ought to he indifferent to the necessities of another section.
There is another subject I would call to the attention of my hon. friend from the West. We have, out of the public treasury, built for their use, at fabulous cost, three railways, designed to move their harvest and bring their produce to the Canadian harbours to be thence shipped overseas.
We are now building also, at their request, a request made to the late administration and repeatedly pressed upon the present Govern-", "ment,-a burdensome railway, the Hudson Bay railway, to afford them a shorter route to the European markets. I would like to know the bottom reason for those railroad constructions. Why are we wasting so much money on the Hudson Bay road)-built only for the benefit of our western countrymen, since neither Ontario nor Quebec nor the Maritime provinces can utilize it; why waste so many millions for those western farmers, if those gentlemen are bent on dealing on the American market? Is that fair? Bet them insist with the Government that a stop be put to that useless expenditure on the Hudson Bay railway. It might be after all to the country's advantage to abandon those undertakings and allow the western people freedom of trade with the United States. One of the previous orators stated that in the West the farmer made no money. It appears to me there is not much patriotism in coming here to make such a declaration. If in the West the farmers do not make money, why then ask so much for colonization, why all this propaganda to draw settlers to a region where results are so deceptive?
I, however, have it in my mind that the farmers of the West coin money much more freely than in the East. Had I spoken in the stead of the hon. member I should' certainly not have delivered myself of such a remark, because it is not in the interest of his province. We all know that for the most part the western agriculturists are well-to-do and that many of them become rich with much less pains than our eastern farmers.
Such are the few remarks I wished to make. I make them without acrimony and m the best possible intention, so that our friends from the West may realize that (hey should not be parties to these unhealthy agitations, that they are not the only inhabitants of this country, but that on the contrary, they have to live in close community with the other parts of Canada, and that their first thought should be the general interests of the country, and not those o.f a particular section.
These remarks, which I have just quoted from my speech of last year, are very fair and very just, and I still believe that the giving of such advantages to our friends of the West is contrary to the interests of the . East. We in the East are ready to support the measure that has been put into force lately by this Government in order to afford an opportunity to our western friends to sell their wheat at a high price; we are ready to make the sacrifice, but on one condition, and it is that these gentlemen immediately cease thinking that Canada exists only for themselves, and that they should remember that there are other parts of the country that want to be protected. With regard to the continual cry for free trade with the United States, while I admit that this will be a benefit for the West, at the same time it is contrary to our interest in the East, and we are solidly against it, and as a patriot I would ask my friends from the West to advise their supporters that they are not TMr. Boulay.]
alone in this country, and that they must bear their share of tiie burdens of nationhood, sharing in the disadvantages as well as the advantages that may result from tariff reform. In the East we are patriots from an economic standpoint as well as from a fighting standpoint. I am sorry to see published in the western papers attacks against the East, and principally against the province of Quebec, for not doing its duty in this great war. Let me tell the House that the county of Rimouski alone has furnished no less than 800 soldiers for overseas, and the neighbouring counties of Bonaventure and Gaspe have, to a large extent, furnished their share. As the representative of the county of Rimouski, which has furnished such a large number of volunteers to our Canadian army, I say that such attacks should not be made. When, the other day, I heard the hon. member for Dufferin (Mr. Best) quote from a paper a letter from an officer who passed through the province of Quebec, charging our people with insulting the soldiers when they were passing through that province, I was really sorry to hear such an unjust accusation. I do not say that my hon. friend made that statement in order to insult us, for, perhaps, he thought that it might be true, but I may assure the House and the people of Canada that in my county and the adjoining counties of Bonaventure and Gaspe, Which have furnished so many soldiers, the people are in entire sympathy with the valiant Canadians who go overseas to defend us.
Whether they come from British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, or any other province we are delighted to see the soldiers going overseas to defend our liberty and fight in the cause of humanity. If there have been any such instances as alleged, I should like to see the facts established, and the responsibility placed where it belongs. It may be that soldiers, just like private citizens, have made mistakes occasionally at some of the railway stations in Quebec, and if they insult the people they must expect to be insulted in return. I know that if the soldiers were insulted at Riviere du Loup and Mont Joli, it would be because of the behaviour of the soldiers themselves, not all of them, but a few. The people had no thought of insulting them until they were provoked. I know of one instance where soldiers have insulted women. In Campbellton, which is not in the province of Quebec, some of them took the liberty of seizing a horse and wagon, shoving the proprietor aside, and taking a ride around

the town. Other soldiers burst into a liquor store in the same town, and took the whole contents. They must naturally expect to be insulted when they do things like that. But these are merely isolated cases, and bad-will must not be imputed to our people, because we are just as patriotic as any of our fellow Canadians and just as eager to win the war. I trust that steps will be taken by the Government or militia authorities to ascertain whether the allegations made by this officer are true, and if an investigation is held I am sure it will be found that his charges are baseless.
I would take this opportunity of asking the newspapers of the West to cease their attacks upon us. Soldiers from the West, who have read these articles in the western newspapers, must be prejudiced against the province of Quebec, and in passing through our province on their way overseas, they are apt to take offence at little things which otherwise would pass unnoticed. As soon as this depreciation of the province of Quebec in our western newspapers ceases, the better it will be for all the people of this country.
In listening to the speeches on the motion by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte), I heard hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House one after the other criticise the Government for not doing so and so. The Government was not doing its duty in trying to meet present conditions, they said. In my opinion these charges are a disgrace to those who preferred them. When we think of the terrible crisis with which the Government is confronted, and of the courage displayed not only by the Government as a whole, but by the distinguished gentleman who presides over the Finance Department, instead of trying ibo deprecate hiim lamid accuse him of not doing his duty, hon. gentlemen opposite should get up and praise him for the ability he has shown in conducting the financial affairs of this country since the beginning of the war. Instead of indulging in criticism of that sort hon. gentlemen should get together and help the Government, regardless of party, to pull through the hard times with which we are confronted. One hon. gentleman opposite asks, What has the Government done since the beginning of the war to meet the situation? It should not be necessary to ask such a question. We had to raise, equip and send overseas in a very short time
400,000	soldiers. The money had to be raised to pay these men, and to meet our
obligations in connection with the war. Besides that, the Government had to carry on the ordinary public services of this country just as in times of peace. The war made the situation confronting the Government ten times harder than anything a government in this country had ever faced before, and I think when hon. gentlemen opposite'think of these things, they should compliment the Government instead of reproaching them.
As a representative of the East, I feel very keenly the hard times through which we are passing. The price of flour we should all be very glad indeed to see come down. Our labourers are confronted with a situation we have never before had in this country, and I am sure that if no other solution of the problem can be found, in order to bring down the price of flour and of meat, our farmers in the East would not grumble if the price of potatoes was cut in half and they received only $1 per bushel. I know, from having talked with several of them, that they would be glad to sell their potatoes at $1 a bushel, provided that the prices of flour and meat were reduced proportionately. I have enough confidence in the Government to believe that if this conclusion can be brought about they will take means to that end. That being so, there is no need for the opposition to criticize and to try to embarrass the situation. For my part, I think the best thing we can do is to act as patriots, to act unanimously, and, if we have suggestions, to make them to the Government, in order that we may be united in carrying on and bringing to a successful conclusion the present terrible war.
On motion of Mr. McKenzie the debate was adjourned.
On the motion of Sir Thomas White, the House adjourned at 11.10 p.m.
Friday, May 4, 1917."]

speechtext: If the statement is correct that 47,000,000 bushels of wheat are at the present time held by the farmers of the Northwest, would my hon. friend also commandeer that, and if so, at what price?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: THE HIGH PRICE OF FLOUR.
subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS QUESTION.
speechtext:
I would commandeer it from any person who entertains the same lack

of consideration for the Canadian consumer that the stock speculators do. The farmers are the growers of wheat; the stock manipulators are not the growers of wheat, but the latter are exacting this undue profit from and they are imposing this undue privation upon the people of Canada simply and solely to enrich themselves. If the Government will commandeer this wheat and will ask the millers upon what terms they will mill and distribute ify and if a satisfactory agreement is not made with the millers, then the Government have the power to take over the mills, mill the wheat themselves and distribute the flour to the consumers in Canada. That is being done in Great Britain. The Government of Great Britain have taken over the mills, in that way guaranteeing to the British consumers that they will have their flour at the lowest possible price consistent with the conditions existing at the present time. Perhaps I may not have succeeded in impressing upon the Minister of Finance the real gravity of the situation as it exists throughout the Dominion and more particularly -as ilt exists in that part of -Canada with which I am most familiar, namely, the Maritime Provinces. I cannot imagine that the Minister of Finance will continue indifferent to the existing situation and I implore him to take immediate and effective steps, not only to prevent any further increase in the price of flour, but to restore the price of flour to that which will be reasonable, having regard to the price which the farmers have received for their wheat. My motion sets forth the necessity of taking action to prevent the undue advance in the price of flour, and the desirability of taking action to prevent further undue advances in the price of flour in Canada and to reduce the same to the amount representing the price of wheat received by the farmers, plus the cost of milling and distributing, but eliminating the increase due to stock exchange manipulation.	_
I do not think there is any hon. gentleman within the hearing of my voice who will state that that is ai) unfair or unreasonable demand. All I ask at the present time is that the element of speculation, for which no return is being given, should he eliminated from the price; that the consumer in Canada should be obliged to pay for his flour only that amount which represents the cost of the wheat to the farmer plus the cost of milling and distribution, but no excess profits to any person who contributes nothing to the production of the

wheat or flour supply of the Dominion of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had intended making a few remarks on the high cost of living before the Budget debate closed, but I will take this opportunity and say what I have to say now. The motion of my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) is, to my mind, a very important one, and I think the Government should take immediate steps to tackle this question. It is all very well for the Minister of Labour to tell us that his officers have been following the price of flour in this country for the last three or four years. So have the consumers, and the officers of the Government have done nothing so far as I can see to remedy the evil. But the time will come, I hope, in the not far distant future, when the consumers of this country will be in a position to remedy this evil. In my humble opinion, the efforts of the Government to reduce the high cost of living in this country are a .mere farce. Several years ago the Department of Labour appointed a commission to investigate the high cost of living, and, after in-.

quiring into conditions for a year or two, the commission presented a very voluminous [DOT]report. The only actual bit of information I could find in that report, and I perused it carefully, was that the price of commodities in this country was generally regulated by the demand for them. During the two years this commission was making its inquiries the price of commodities in this country was rising higher and higher. I do not remember this commission ever telling the Government or the people of this country how they were going to reduce the cost of living. Since then commission after commission has been appointed by the Department of Labour to investigate the cause of the increase ins the price of the necessaries of life throughout the Dominion. The trouble is, Mr. Speaker, that these commissions, which the people of this country have to pay for, are doing no good. They gather a lot of information which is never acted upon. What will be the result of the visit of the officers of the Department of Labour to Montreal to-day, for example? Will the Department of Labour take,some action that will result in the people being able to get flour for less than the present prices? Or will they simply send in reports and allow prices to continue ito soar?

I am not interested in the price at Chicago. What I am interested in is the price at which the consumers of this country are paying for flour. The hon. gentleman can follow out that proportion. But the strong point after all is that the millers of this country are not paying $2.80, neither are they paying $3, neither are they paying $1.80 for the wheat out of which they are making the flour for which they are charging the consumers $14.50 per barrel. The great bulk of the flour that they are selling to the people at $14.50 a barrel is flour ground from wheat bought in February or last fall at $1.13, $1.59 and $1.78 a bushel. They have in their possession at the present time sufficient wheat, according to their own statistics, to keep them going for the next three or four months. Yet, they are charging the people $14.50 a barrel for flour when the wheat out of which that flour was made cost them fifty per cent less than wheat is costing to-day. The Minister of Finance admitted the other day that the millers had been making more money than any other class of manufacturers. If they have been doing that, is it just and fair that they should be allowed to continue to do so in view of the fact that they are not paying this high price for wheat? Is it fair that they should be allowed to raise the price of flour to the people of this country to a point which will make it almost impossible for the great majority to have flour in their possession at all? Of course, it is most humiliating that we should have had from the Minister of Labour a statement of the large amounts of wheat produced in Russia. He tells us, of course, that the figures from Russia are very interesting. That is something that will be most consoling to the housewives throughout Canada when they complain to their husbands that flour is $14.50 a barrel and that there is a possibility of it going to $20. Somebody will say to them: The Minister of Labour says that the figures with reference to wheat from Russia .are very interesting, you must look at the long strings of figures which the Minister of Labour brought down to show that you are
not in need of wheat and flour at all and that it is all right to pay $14.50 a 'barrel for your flour, although labouring men are only making $1.25 or $2 per day. If the labouring classes of this country were getting sufficient pay to enable them to buy these commodities at the present high rates, my voice would not be heard in Parliament to protest against the prevailing prices. But, they are not. There is only one class of labourers who are getting wages somewhat proportionate to what they are- paying for the necessaries of life, and tho-se are the people who are working in the munition factories. They are getting good wages.

Well, I am not. I am sorry -if my hon. friend is -being imposed upon by some coal dealer in Nova Scotia because the coal dealers are not getting those prices. The coal companies have not doubled up, have not increased their prices by fifty per cent or forty per cent or twenty-five per -cent. If my hon. friend will take the trouble to compare the

prices that the Department of Railways and Canals are paying for their coal at the present time with the prices which they paid last year, and the year befpre, he will see that the amounts I stated are perfectly correct.
I have taken up more time on this subject than I had intended but it is a most serious question. It is a question which should demand the immediate attention of the Ministry of this country. There may be difficulties, there may be troubles, in the way, but we are living in troublesome times. The problem may need an extraordinary remedy but we are living in extraordinary times. I have to plead not only for the general consumer in this country hut for the wives and children of the men who have gone to the front. Many of these men were getting very good wages before leaving their homes to fight for King and country. They are getting to-day, I need not tell this House, $1.10 per day, their wives are getting $20 per month separation allowance, if they are privates, and most of them are privates, and they may also he getting a little from the Patriotic Fund which is a God-send in itself. But, at the same time, if for no other reason than the fact that we have thousands and hundreds of thousands of men at the front who have left families, large in number and small in stature, and who are receiving not fifty per cent of the wages that they get in times of peace, this Government should be loyal fo these men and see to it that their wives and children should not be left to starve on the mere pittance they are getting and that the millers of this country should not be permitted to impose on them to the extent of a 100 per cent advance in a few months in the price of flour.
Of those who went to the front from the town of Glace Bay, from which I come, I am sorry to say there are 176 on the death roll. That is a large number for a comparatively small town. There are 176 graves on the fields of France of men who enlisted from my town, and a great proportion of these were married men. I know to my sorrow that these women have had a hard time to struggle on, and they will have an equally hard time under the present pension system, which, after all, is fairly good as compared with other pension systems. But I think that the Government of this country should take some steps to see that these people at least, who are all consumers and dependents on this Government,

are hot further imposed upon by the manipulators, the contractors, and especially the millers of this country, who I think have imposed upon the public at least in their present exorbitant advance in the price of flour.

Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to take part in this debate to-day, and I should not have done so had it not been for the very unfair method followed by the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. W. H. Bennett) in his remarks concerning myself. There was a time when I should not have expected very much better than this from the member for East Simcoe, but I must say that during the last five or six years he has given considerable evidence of being a gentleman. I am surprised, therefore, at his conduct this afternoon.
It is a fact that I belonged to the Militia of Canada for a number of years down to about seven or eight years before war broke out in 1914. I belonged to the Field Artillery. The time came when I must either take command of my battery or retire, and as I was too busy to take command of the battery, I retired. The facts will be found in the Militia List, and there is no question as to them. At the time of the declaration of war I was 52 years of age, and I was too old to enlist as a private, so I went to the Minister of Militia and offered my services, if they were of any use to him, as an officer, and asked for the right to raise a battery of field artillery. This occurred during the month of August, 1914, about three weeks after the declaration of war. Nothipg further came of the matter until the latter part of April, 1915, when the minister started a correspondence with me which was carried on for some time, all the documents except one being marked "confidential." I got a little suspicious that I was not being treated by the minister as though he wanted my services, and therefore I wrote him on the 4th of September, 1915, a letter which is not marked "confidential," which must be in the public files of the Militia Department and which I propose now reading to the House, and when I have done so, I have no further comment to make upon it. The remainder of the file is marked "confidential"; it is in the hands of either the present Minister of Militia or the ex-Minister of Militia, and as they are both alive and on the earth, they can produce the remainder of the correspondence. I have here all the original letters received by me from the minister and copies of the letters written by me to

105a
him. This letter was written on the 4th day of September, 1915, being the day when the ex-Minister of Militia returned from his trip to England during that summer:
Woodstock, N.B., September 4, 1915. Major-General Sir Sam Hughes,
Ottawa.
My dear Sir Sam:
I wrote you last re my request to be allowed to recruit a battery of Field Artillery on July 2, and on July 8 received an acknowledgment from Col. Winter, stating that * inquiries were being made regarding my appointment, and as soon as a reply was received, I would be communicated with." I have heard nothing from that date, and nearly two months have now gone by. If anything is to be done, there is no time to lose, especially as I would not want to raise a battery to remain in_ Canada during the coming winter. If you think ^ well of my proposition, and as I read the times, the Empire needs all the help possible, I tiust you will set the machinery in motion at once, and if nothing; comes of it, then please let me know and I will know what to do.
Believe me, sincerely yours,
(Sgd.) F. B. Carvell.
The reply to that, also marked "confidential," was received by me on the 10th day of November, 1915, or two months and one week after my letter was written. While I cannot give the contents of the answer, it is needless to say it was not an acceptance of my proposition or I would not be here to-day, because, without casting any reflection upon any other member of this House, I may say that when I made a proposition to raise a battery of Field Artillery I intended to raise it not to leave it in England but to stay with it to the end, and that end probably meant forever so far as I was concerned. I have nothing more to say, but that I am rather sorry that my hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. W. H. Bennett), who has been in this House with me for many years, thought it was his business to refer to a personal matter of this kind; but as he has done so, I believe I am justified in giving this much information to the House.

I had some potatoes, and when the price reached $1.75 a bag I sold them, because I was ashamed to keep them any longer, and I think I got more than they were worth, and if my neighbours got that much they did pretty well, too. It is not, however, a question what price I would say. I say, under war conditions, with prices soaring, with many people finding it almost impossible to make a living, it is not a question of how much the farmers could get, or would get; it is a question of the duty of the Government to take these matters up and grapple with them as men would do, from the standpoint of fair prices and fair profits. The British Gpvemiment did not hesitate to grapple with these questions. Within the last five months we have seen in the Old Country newspapers such statements as: You shall not sell such and such a commodity at more than a certain price. This Government, only two months ago, took that attitude in Tegard to newsprint; they

said to the newsprint manufacturers: Ypu shall not 'chafge beyond a certain price and the newsprint manufacturers submitted. The whole difference is this. The newsprint is sold entirely to the newspapers publishers of Canada, and the newspapers of Canada were in a position so to bombard the Minister of Finance that he was compelled to comply with their request, and when sufficient pressure was put uppn him he had no hesitation; there were no lions in the path; there were no constitutional difficulties; he had the War Measures Act and under it he said to the newsprint manufacturers: You must sell this paper at a certain price, or I will make you. Those gentlemen at once complied with the request and are selling the paper to-day at that price. I believe this matter of the price of foodstuffs comes within the Department of Labour, but I have grave doubts of his settling it. At all events, the Government as a whole might say to those! in Canada who have wheat or potatoes in store-I do not care whether they are producers ,or middlemen-you must sell them at a fair price. Down in the Maritime Provinces we are paying forty to forty-five cents a pound for bacon. Why cannot the Government say to the men who have thousands of pounds of bacon stored away in the storage houses:	You must sell
that bacon at a fair price. Why cannot they say to the men who have meats and food products of all kinds store ! away, and who have been gambling with the necessities of the people in order to make exorbitant profits, "You must sell these articles at a fixed price." The thing is all very simple. A great many things have been done in this old world within the last few years that people said could not be done before, and perhaps a great many things which would not have been thought justifiable before. But to-day this old world is at war, and thousands of people in Canada are barely able to keep body and soul together. There are women and children in this country who have not tasted meat for a fortnight, and that is true of all our cities and towns. They have not the means with which to buy meat or potatoes. In view of these conditions, why should not the Government interfere? If the Government have not the nerve to interfere, why do they not make way for men who would?

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to take part in this debate, but the subject under consideration is an exceedingly important one, and it seems to me just as well that the opportunity has been afforded of discussing here to-day not only the high price of flour, but the high cost of living generally. We are living in most serious times, the most serious in our history, and I believe in the history of the world. I do not suppose that at any time in human history has there been so much dislocation of commerce as at present. There has never been a time of such profound change; never a time in which there has been so much human suffering in 'the world and so much anxiety, or when public opinion was so sensitive, and subjected to such severe strain as to-day. This is a time when governments charged with the responsibility of carrying on the affairs of a country are the subject of much criticism. It is proper that governments should be subjected to fair criticism, but I believe it to be the duty of the opposition in any House such as this, to approach a question such as is now under consideration, judicially, fairly, and in a statesmanlike manner, and not with the object of making-political capital out of it at a time like

this. I propose, therefore, to discuss this question somewhat at length, as it is a question that should be discussed, and discussed fairly. If the Government is at fault with regard to the high cost of living,
I want to know it, and in what respect, and if it can be shown that we are at fault we shall endeavour to the best of our ability to rectify what may be wrong. Where are we when we have done that? The hon. gentleman did not pause to inquire how many bushels of wheat make a barrel of flour. Well, it takes a little less than four and a. half bushels. He vould commandeer wheat at |2.80 or $3 a.bushel. Four and a half times $3 would be $13.50; so that the wheat alone would cost as much as the flour costs to-day. That is the beautiful suggestion he puts forward for the serious consideration, of this House. I do not think it is necessary for me to say anything more on that head; the members of this House are too intelligent-when they get away from politics-not to know that flour has gone up in price because wheat has gone up in price. And why have the prices of wheat and of every other commodity in Canada gone up-yes, every other commodity in the world? I propose to tell the House why, in my opinion, prices have gone up. Unless we take account of what has happened in the world, we shall not be able to discuss this question intelligently.
The world to-day is at war. Twenty-five millions of men are under arms, taken from industries of all kinds and. now devoting their energies to mutual slaughter. The first effect of that is to cause a shortage of labour, and the effect of that in turn is an increase in wages-an increase not only in those .countries that are at war but in every country. This results in an increase in the price of every commodity which is produced by labour, that is, every commodity in the world, including, of course, agricultural products. More than that, the cost of capital-interest-has gone up. And interest is a factor in price. Interest has gone up because the great governments of the world are pouring out floods of securities in order to raise money to carry on the war. They have taken possession of the market. In Great Britain industrial concerns are not allowed, except under special circumstances, to raise money by the sale of securities. Securities that used to be sold on a two and a half per cent basis are now sold on a five, six and seven per cent basis, and in the case of some foreign governments, their securities are sold on the basis of eight and nine per cent. This is another
cause of increase, in the cost of production. Again, the withdrawal of these millions of men from the fields prevents cultivation of the soil from being carried on upon anything like the scale on which it was carried on before the war. Not only is cultivation not so extensive, but it is not so efficient as it was. And a great deal of territory formerly under cultivation is ravaged by war and is not under cultivation to-day. All this affects supply-and demand and supply regulate pi ices. Another important feature in relation to supply is the shortage of tonnage. The world's transportation system is dislocated. The whole food supply of Australia is shut 5 p.m. up by reason of the submarine menace and the shortage of shipping. The hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) had the temerity to criticise the Minister of Labour because prices were lower in Australia than in Canada. What is the reason for that difference? Australia is four times as far from Great Britain as Canada is, and freights and insurance are greatly increased. Then tljere is the shortage of tonnage. The hon. member for Brookville (Mr. Webster), who made one of the best speeches I ever hbard in this House, pointed out that New Zealand had
400,000	boxes of cheese, and, as I recollect it, 3,500,000 carcases of mutton for which she could not-get transportation. What must be the effect upon local prices? Of course, local prices must be lower than in England, or Canada, or the United States.
Now, there is one point I wish to make, and to make it clearly. You cannot compare this country with England. This is an exporting country, like the United States. We raise wheat and other farm products for export. My hon. friend points out what they have done in England, in taking possession of supplies. But England is in an entirely different position from ourselves, for it is an importing country.

I will come to that. I usually finish up a question before I get through, I believe, and I will try to do that on this occasion. I have shown that the food supply of the world has been greatly diminished by reason of conditions arising out of the war. I failed to mention that the supplies of Russian wheat have not reached their usual market by reason of the closing of the Dardanelles. So much, for the side of supply.
Now, what about demand? While supply has fallen off, demand has increased. Why? One reason is that the armies in this war are better fed than armies ever were before in the history of the world. There are thousands, if not millions, of men, especially in the continental armies, who are better fed to-day than they have ever been fed in their lives before-many of those that were en-gage*d in industrial life are very much better fed. Consequently, the demand for food for these armies is very great. In addition, the high wages paid to workers in munitions and other industries mean that the people have money to spend. Besides that, there is less unemployment in the world than ever before in the lifetime of any man in this House. And the people, having good wages, spend more for food than they did before. The hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick (Mr. Carvell) talks of the '*'misery" in this country at the present time. There never was a time in our history when there was less unemployment and less distress than there is at this moment. I give my word that since this war broke out-or, at least since a few months after its outbreak, because there was a complete dislocation of business in the early days of the war-it has never been suggested to me in my public position that there was any real distress.

The hon. member (Mr. Carvell) poses here as the tribune of the common people. I have as much sympathy with the common people as he has- I ought to, because I am one of them myself. They are the best people in the world, and that is the reason why the Lord made so many of them. As I was saying: there is greater demand from the armies and greater demand from the European centres of population where the people are earning higher wages than before. This is another reason besides the shortage of supply, why the cost of commodities has risen. It is a world condition. Now, I am not speaking about combines. If there are combines and monopolies to enhance prices, that is an entirely different matter, and is to be considered by itself; I am speaking of the ordinary conditions under which the farmers of this country work.
Prices are determined by the laws of supply and demand, by world laws which it is within the power of no Government 'to wholly control. Great Britain herself tried to do it in regard to sugar at the outbreak of the war and signally failed. The British Government's effort to deal with the sugar question was a failure. The hon. member for Richmond says that it is due to wheat manipulation. There Is an element of truth in that but it is not nearly so great as my hon. friend suggests. I accept the disclaimer of my hon. friend from Carleton. But how ban you absolutely ignore market conditions for wheat in Chicago and Minneapolis when you are dealing with the prices in Canada? There is an approximation between the prices at Winnipeg and Chicago. It is true, there may be a corner or something of that kind at one place or the other but the condition created in that way is only temporary. Suppose you undertook to fix the price in Canada? Suppose you said that you would not allow a higher price in Canada than $1.50 a bushel at a time when you are appealing to the western farmer to raise more grain? Here is a point I desire to make: Things tend in this world to cure themselves. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) who is one of the best economists in this

House, would, I think, agree with me in saying that if you have a high price for anything the tendency is for industry and capital to flow into that particular industry and to remedy the situation. If farming is profitable, farming will be prosecuted. My own opinion is that the prevailing high prices are more than likely to be ameliorated by the farmer feeling that he is getting a fair price for his labour than they would be if we were to step in and say: No, you must take an artificial price.
- Suppose you fixed a price for wheat in this country lower than it is in the United States, would the farmer in the West sow his grain this spring for the harvest next fall? Would he not rather say: I will go to some place where I can get the world price for my wheat? Would he not say: I will go across the line and engage in farming.
I am indicating some of the difficulties in dealing with this question. It seems to be a very simple question for hon. gentlemen opposite. Do hon. gentlemen opposite say: Take away from the farmer the world price, cut it in half? The farmer might very well say: Why should I be put in such a position of disadvantage in an exporting country? I doubt very much if hon. gentlemen opposite would suggest that the farmer should be deprived of the fair world's price for his product. The hon. member from Brockville (Mr. Webster) showed the House conclusively the other night that the cost to the farmer for labour and for the commodities which he uses has greatly increased. We cannot therefore say to the farmer: You must take the price that you get in ordinary and normal times, notwithstanding the fact that your cost has increased. I do not believe there is an hon. gentleman opposite who would dare get up and say that to the farming community and I think it would be a most unwise course for the Government to pursue.

I do not know
what kind of farmers my hon. friend has in his district, but I have no doubt there are a lot of honest men there. I will say that I have neveT known the farmers of this or any other community to obtain profits to which they thought they were not reasonably entitled because I know how hard they work. I have worked on a farm and I have worked in an office. I have heard people talk about the heavy responsibility that men have in offices but I take notice that an hon. gentleman like my hon. friend from Carleton, and myself, and the rest of us, would very much rather have the responsibility, with six hours a day in an office, than get up at five o'clock in the morning and finish at eight o'clock with the very slender profits derived by the farmer. It is all right enough for hon. gentlemen opposite to attack the farmers but while I am just as much interested as any body in reducing the high cost of living I maintain that the farmers of this country are entitled to a fair deal.
My hon. friend asked: What about the millers? And he spoke about the large profits of the millers. I would like to point out to my hon. friend that the Government have not been unmindful of its duties regarding the millers. Of all the profits that the millers make, and they have been pretty large in the last two or three years, the Government steps in and takes a large portion by virtue of the business profits war tax. I will point to another thing, and I do so because after all we should deal with these matters fairly and try to reach a sound conclusion. The profits of a particular industry may be large, but they may



bear a very small relationship to, indeed, they may be only a fraction of one per cent of, the volume of business transacted. I should not be at all surprised if all the profits derived by the millers of this country would be a very small percentage indeed of the increase of the price which has taken place in regard to flour. If I were arguing this with the idea only of political expediency, it is possible that I would not say this, but I think it is desirable that in this House we should ascertain the truth. What is the fact? If my hon. friend would distribute all the profits made by the milling companies in Canada over the cost of living in Canada, they would represent an exceedingly small percentage indeed. I am not in sympathy with these large profits at all. I like to see men make fair profits, but it must be borne in mind that traders, keen traders, capable men, even under world conditions, that are not subject to control by combines, make large profits.
As long as there are no combines, as long as there is no monopoly, as a general thing you do more harm than good when you interfere. But what a Government could do and what this Government has done is to say to people who make enormous profits in war time: Gentlemen, we are going to take away from you a very substantial portion of those excess profits for the prosecution of the war. Hon. gentlemen have charged the Government with not reducing the cost of living. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers), I know, has used his best endeavours in this most difficult matter. We have accomplished something. It is not possible for any Government to accomplish very much with respect to the reduction of the cost of living. At all events, I have never seen a practical suggestion put forward, apart from that one question: Is there a monopoly, is there a trust, is there a combine? If you have a monopoly, a combine, a trust, then something can be done by a Government in order to take away the undue advantage which a trust or combine or monopoly possesses. But, generally speaking, outside of that, the laws of supply and demand govern. Left us see what the situation is in regard to the United States, a question raised by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). What is our position? Here we have a boundary line of 3,600 miles from east to west, with their products flowing over to U3 and ours flowing over to them. Can you fix the price of wheat in Canada without the price being fixed in

the United States also? Does my hon. friend think that if you fixed the price of wheat at Winnipeg at $1.25 a bushel it would at once affect Chicago to the same extent? It would mean that the business of Canada would be done in Chicago.

No, it is not polities. I will tell you what was politics, the suggestion that this Government is blam-able for the manipulation by speculators on the Chicago and the Winnipeg exchanges was politics; and if it was not politics, I will tell you what else it was not, it was not sense. I would like to make one more observation about the Winnipeg situation. The committee of the Winnipeg Exchange took steps a short time ago to prevent the speculation to which my hon friend refers;
I tell him now that so far as Winnipeg is concerned, I have reason to believe that these price fluctuations are not due to manipulation in the sense he puts forward to-day. I will tell him to what they are due, because some of us go into thdse questions more deeply than the hon. member for Richmond. The principal buying in Winnipeg and even on the other side of the line is on behalf of the British Commission, and what I think is that the export buying of these contract grades has about exhausted the available amount, and the result is that others who have contracted for wheat are working on a much narrower margin than before. And I will tell my
hon. friend another thing, that if we commandeered all the wheat in this country, most of the wheat we would commandeer in the West would be wheat that is owned by the British Government and bought by the British Government for the purposes of the people of Great Britain. That is the wheat he wants us to take away from them.
My hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) does* not realize, when he approaches a world question like this, that it cannot be dealt with so flippantly as to say: Why does not the Government reduce the price from $3 to $1.25? That is the unfair feature of charges brqught by hon. gentlemen opposite against this Government, especially in a time like this. We all realize that this is a serious question, the question of the high price of flour, the high cost of living generally. We all realize that, but the world is out of joint. The world is upside down. And the unfairness of it is aggravated by the fact that, the country being at war, the public mind is under a great strain and speeches such as we have heard, unless the facts are presented at the same time, are apt to disturb the public mind and to create a most erroneous, a most unfair impression as to the Government and its powers over the price of commodities.
It was only for the purpose of clearing up the situation and indicating the conditions which underlie world prices, that I have risen to my feet. In a way, I am glad that it has come up, not only because we are able to meet the charges of the members for Richmond (Mr. Kyte), South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) and Carleton, N.B., (Mr. Carvell) but also in order that this discussion may to some extent inform the people as to the conditions Which have brought about these high prices, from which we all suffer, but over which even governments have comparatively limited powers of control.

Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) was more interested in making a defence of the Government against real and imaginary criticisms than he was to deal with the critical situation now confronting the people of Canada and, indeed, most of the countries of the world. I am sure that the House is grateful to the member for Richmond (Mr. G. W. Kyte) for having introduced by his resolution a subject which, as the Minister of Finance says, is exceedingly

grave. Hon. gentlemen, in this House should he glad to avail themselves of the opportunity-indeed, should he glad that the hon. member for Richmond has presented the opportunity to them,-of discussing a problem which is serious, which is world-wide, and which will he a grave question for several years to come.
The Minister of Finance complains that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House have interjected a political tinge into the debate. I deny that most emphatically. I heard the remarks of the hon. membeT for Richmond, the member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) and the member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) and I am within the judgment of the House when I say that every fact presented by these hon. gentlemen was relevant to the resolution. Who interjected politics into this debate? Did not hon. gentlemen on the other side interject small politics, personalities and irrelevant issues into the discussion of a matter that is of paramount importance to the people whom we represent?
I agree with the Minister of Finance when he says that this is a very serious question and that we should discuss it in a serious way, in the hope that some light may be thrown, upon the problem and that some advantage may accrue as a result of our deliberations. What I complain of respecting the Government and hon. gentlemen opposite is that while they admit the existence of the problem, they do not give evidence of any effort to procure a solution. The Minister of Labour read us a great array of figures which were known, in a general way, to every member of this House and to everybody in the country. The figures may 'be interesting, but only in an academio sense, whereas the cost of the necessaries of life is a practical question. The Minister of Labour produced figures showing that the world's production of wheat was much less than that of one or two year's ago. Well, that was a mathematical proof of one of the causes of the problem confronting the country. He ended his 'speech, however, without proffering any suggestion or telling us what his department was doing in the premises. In fact, he displayed no interest whatever in that question. He informed us that an officer of his department was sent to Montreal this afternoon. What has that to do with the question? Of what possible interest can the departure of that official from this city be to this House? It would be just a6 in-
teresting had he informed Uo of his having dispatched that officer of his department on an aeroplane flight three or four miles above this city. This is the theatre of action for the Department of Labour; here is where the minister and his officers should work. The dispatch, of his official to Montreal, while stated in very serious fashion by the minister, cannot but be regarded as a deliberate evasion of a serious question.
I should like to emphasize what the Minister of Finance said this afternoon, that a very serious problem confronts us. If the Government would sincerely view it in that aspect, they would endeavour to do something to 'meet the situation. It may be difficult to secure from people generally the interest which this subject justifies, because we are blinded by an artificial prosperity, and our perspective is out of focus. Nevertheless, the problem before us, while recognized as acute at the present time, is well known to be a problem which will stay with us for many years. As the Minister of Finance has properly remarked, the labour of 25,000,000 people has been transferred from productive spheres into war fields. That condition necessarily involves a dislocation of the economics of the world, and imposes serious responsibilities upon us charged with the administration of public affairs.
In some countries the seriousness of prevailing conditions is realized. In England the seriousness of the situation in Great Britain was recently impressed upon the public by Lord Davenport, who, I think, is Controller of Foodstuffs. They are even contemplating the destruction of dogs and the rationing of horses; the 24th day of this month is being set aside for the making of a nation-wide appeal against waste. These things all indicate serious thought on the part of the people in that country. So important do they regard the shortage of wheat and the high price of flour that they are seriously considering the abandonment of meatless days, which are causing a greater strain to be made upon the bread supply. Take the United States; are they not exhibiting a more intelligent and active interest in this question than we are, although, perhaps, there is less reason for their doing so than we of Canada? An investigation is now being conducted before the United States Trade Commission, assisted by the Department of Agriculture. Forty states of the American Union are represented in that convention. They recognize the seriousness of conditions

there; there has been a failure of the winter wheat crop.
There has also been a failure of the winter crop in Canada. The weather prevailing in the past few days is regarded as a very serious matter by wheat growers in this country,, and if the unfavourable weather conditions of the past week continue, the result may be very serious. These unfavourable weather conditions seem to be recognized more keenly and acutely in all other parts of the world than they are in Canada. The question of the shortage of flour and the high price of bread is very serious; it is a more serious one for the industrial classes than for the well-to-do classes, who can substitute other foodstuffs for bread, but bread is the staple foodstuff of the industrial classes and it is necessary that they have sufficient bread to maintain industrial efficiency. The high price of foodstuffs affects the whole social and economic fabric of this and all countries. It aggravates social unrest; it intensifies the labour difficulties of the country. The Minister of Finance asks what can be done; he proclaims to us that the Government are willing to do anything if the way is . pointed out to them. Many things might be done and should have been done long ago, aye, even years ago. Desperate diseases require desperate remedies. We all know, as does the Minister of Finance, the general conditions that in normal times affect the prices of all commodities. There are the causes of demand and supply, transportation, waste, extravagance, the cost of high living and other things. These are well known to the world. There is available to every one who chooses to read it a wealth of literature which will give him in all amplitude the general reasons and causes for high prices of foodstuffs in normal times. But we are not living in normal times, and in order to meet the conditions, measures, which in ordinary times might be considered quite radical, must be taken. That is the only way in which we can meet the situation with success. Everything that is uneconomical and unlawful should be prevented by law, and we should not hesitate to take action. Anything that tends to the withdrawal of products from the markets of the country is in some degree preventable. There is nothing wrong in our endeavouring to control by license or by some other method every one who is engaged in the manufacture, transportation, sales, storage or distribution of food. This cannot be done effectually by any one formula, but there vis surely some remedy available to 'the Government if they chose to study the situation carefully and were fully seized of the seriousness of it, and if they really desired to ameliorate conditions. Under certain circumstances the Government would be fully justified by the people of this country in fixing prices; there would be no objection to the Government taking absolutely under their control the flour mills of this1 country. What possible objection could there be to that in all the circumstances prevailing to-day? Would there be any objection to the Government taking control in certain localities of our railway systems, so as to effect a more direct and effective control over transportation and rates? There is no limit to what thq Government might not attempt to do if it were fully seized of the seriousness of conditions. I have followed very carefully what the Government have done during the past two or three years with respect to these matters, and I say emphatically, seriously and honestly that there has not come to my notice any single effort in this direction on their part, which I consider indicates a lively and intelligent interest therein. I do not think the Department of Agriculture has been alive to the situation in this country since the beginning of the war, it has carried on no propaganda throughout the Dominion in regard to the matter of production. We have had the Minister of Finance and a few other hon. members during Parliament intermittently stating:	We
want production and more production, but that does not mean anything; that does not produce results. We can produce results by propaganda, but it must be properly organized; it must be energetically and intelligently carried on, not spasmodically and in restricted localities, it must be nation-wide and carried on persistently, and systematically from one end of the country to the other. No man will say in this House that the efforts made by the Department of Labour in this connection have been intelligent or serious. I do not like to say of any public administrator that his work lacks sincerity, but one is compelled to use that expression in regard to the work of the Department of Labour in respect to this matter. The Minister of Finance gave to the House this afternoon the general and fundamental reasons for the high price of commodities, and in a general way he was correct. But why did he not tell that

to the Minister of Labour a year or more ago? Why did he go to the expense of appointing commissions which never investigate and which never will report-and it is just as well they do not report, as their reports at this late date would be absolutely useless, because conditions change so rapidly these days that one can hardly predicate upon existing facts an opinion to-day that would be worth anything to-morrow. The Department of Labour should be active-and the country expects it to be active-upon this question. The Minister of Finance complains that the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) charged the Government with stock manipulations in the wheat market. I deny that. I think that was rather an unjust, an incorrect imputation against the hon. member, and I certainly did not understand him to say that to-day.

speechtext:
I accept the explanation of the Minister of Finance. Nevertheless, he did seek in some form or another to leave the impression on this House that for political purposes, and he emphasized "political purposes," the hon. member for Richmond in speaking to his resolution, connected the Administration with' wheat market speculations. The Minister of Finance says it is unfair to charge the Government with the high prices prevailing to-day. That is a fair statement for him to make, and in a sense it was absolutely unnecessary for him to make it, for we do not think the Government are absolutely bl aim able for the high prices prevailing throughout Canada to-day. But we do say that in many oases the high prices are preventable, and might be modified. We do not ascribe to hon. gentlemen opposite divine powers. We recognize that their limitations are very, very great indeed; but great as they are, we say that if they would only 
display a more active interest in these matters, they could not help bringing about an improvement in the conditions which we are discussing and which bear so heavily on the great mass of our people to-day. It is true that there is prosperity in this Dominion, but it is largely an artificial prosperity, and there are thousands of people to-day in this country who are living either just on or below the poverty line. They are earning large wages, it is true, but the purchasing power of that wage is much below the purchasing power of their wage some few years ago, when it was considerably lower. We are not as prosperous as would appear on the surface, and the Government should not let themselves be lulled to sleep by the fact that wages are high. They should not fail to recognize that the question involved in the resolution introduced by the ihon. member for Richmond this afternoon is a very serious one, and deserving of their most serious consideration and drastic action. If it should mean fixing minimum and maximum prices, let us have it. If it means the taking over of the flour mills of this country, let that be done. If it means a more direct and effective control of the transportation agencies in this country, I say let that be done. If it means the closing of the wheat exchanges of this country, let that be done, although to my mind that might be a very doubtful procedure.
I should also like to enquire why the Government was not in consultation long ago with the Government of the United States on this question. It is all very well for the Minister of Finance to say that at this moment the Minister of Trade and Commerce is in consultation with the British and French Commissions and with the Government of the United States. I venture to say that the Minister of Trade and Commerce would not be in the United States at all if he were not there on the invitation of the British Commission. Instead, he would be wasting his time, as he has been doing for the last two or three years on some abstract questions from which the people of this country can expect nothing in the wdy of results. If the United States and Canada could but act together they would exert a tremendous influence in settling this problem in some degree, not only on this continent, but throughout the whole world. Though the Minister of Trade and Commerce is at Washington, his time no doubt is taken up with many other questions. This problem alone is big enough for any one man, or for

many men, to study, and I think it should be taken up as a special and distinct question with the United States, and a joint commission be appointed by the two countries to study and deal with the whole problem.
I shall not detain the House any longer. I think hon. gentlemen should he grateful to the hon. member for Richmond for having introduced this subject. It is one, I think, we should have discussed in this House long before now. If it might appear that we upon this side of the House are discussing this matter in rather a censorious spirit we may be forgiven because we think that that is the only method by which we can urge this Government to action. We would like hon. gentlemen opposite to participate in this debate, giving friendly advice to the Government and exhorting them to the accomplishment of the results which hon. gentlemen opposite, I am sure, feel this country desires to see attained.

speechtext:
No resolution could be more timely or opportune than the one we are now discussing, for the high cost of living is the burning question now before the people. Of course, there are many to whom that question is comparatively unimportant, because their incomes are sufficient to enable them easily to provide for their wants, but to the average mechanic and labouring man it becomes a very serious and pressing problem, especially in view of the possibility of even the higher prices in the future. But I believe that this problem is one that the Government can deal with. The workers who are called upon to increase production are responding nobly. When at home at last week-end, I found that a number of men had taken up the question of cultivating garden plots in the city of Chatham. But one of these gentlemen, who, by the way, works at his regular occupation from seven in the morning until six at night, brought to my attention one serious handicap under which those engaged in these operations must work. If they send to the United States for seeds, as many of them do, believing that they can get a better class of seeds for their purpose, they have to pay specially high duties. On seeds in packages weighing over one pound each the preferential tariff is five per cent, and
the general tariff ten per cent. But when the packages weigh less than one pound each, the duty from the United States is 25 per cent, with the addition of 74 per cent war tax, making 324 per cent altogether. Most of these people order less than one pound of any one kind of seed, and so they have to pay this higher duty. In order to be sure of the matter I took it up with the Commissioner of Customs, and he gave me these figures. These people naturally ask how it comes that, with everybody urging them to increase production, they should be put under this handicap when they seek to comply with the demand..
The high cost of foodstuffs is particularly the problem of the labouring man, and we hear it on every side from men of this class that the Government is not in sympathy with them. We hear it said that the Government is made up largely of millionaires who do not feel the pressure of the present high prices. It is said also that the Minister of Labour (Hon. Mr. Crothers) is a man not in sympathy with the workers. He may be a gentleman, so far as that is concerned, but he is a professional man, they say, and never did a day's work in his life, and knows nothing of the needs of the labouring man. I have heard that said by many labouring men. It is a point which any future Government in this country will be called upon to consider. Whoever may be at the head of that Government, it will be necessary to have a practical man as Minister of Labour, because the labouring men are going to have something to say about that matter. But we leave that to the electors for the time coming.
Many believe that the prices of foodstuffs are unduly raised through the action of cold storage concerns. When a fire took place in one of these establishments in Lindsay, it was shown that there were thousands of dozens of eggs stored there, as well as other foodstuffs. These were not put on the market, but were held for high prices and exorbitant profits. That is something that, it seems to me, the Government could regulate. Of course, no person will dispute the advantage of the cold storage system; but, on the other hand, nobody will say that that system should be made the means of holding foodstuffs back from the people for unduly high prices. It is a subject of general complaint that the prices of bacons and hams are exorbitant. But it will be , remembered that while there was a large crop of producing hogs last year, there was

a great shortage of feed. The result was that the farmers had to take almost any prices they could get for stock which, if it were in existence flow, would help to keep down prices. This is a case where the Minister of Agriculture was sleeping on his job. In the part of Ontario in which I live, this problem of shortage of feed for hogs was a very serious one, hut the minister never once visited that section that he might find out how the people were placed. Government reports inform us that fifteen per cent of the grain crop of the West was practically unfit for market as grain. But, though we needed it so badly for feed, we could not get it, and so, as I have said, had to dispose of hogs at far less than their real value. And the same was true, to a large extent, of cattle. In the county of Kent dozens and hundreds of cattle were sold at low prices because the farmer could not get feed for them if he wished to hold them over. Had the Minister of Agriculture taken his duties seriously, and had he kept in touch with the wants of the producers, he could have taken steps which would have resulted in a vastly better situation for the consumer to-day. The Minister of Agriculture has not visited that part of the province of Ontario west of Toronto except on one occasion, and that was to address a political meeting. The Department of Agriculture should be largely non-political, and the head of it should keep in touch with the affairs of the country. But how can he do this unless he keeps going around among the people? Let me give one instance of how this shortage in feed worked out. One farmer in the township of Dover sold a part of his farm and gave the money to one son to move west, while the other son stayed on the home farm. The brother who remained at home wanted feed for his animals. The brother who had gone west had the material to spare. But when the westerner tried to ship the material there was an embargo that would prevent it coming east of Fort William. So the man in Kent county had to sell his stock at sacrifice prices. I believe that the Government should have seen to it that such an embargo was not placed on feed coming east of Fort William, considering how much it was in the interest of the country that that material should he transported to where it was so much needed. We are told that there was no rolling stock to be had, but I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that at the very time when we were told they could not get cars

to bring in feed for the stock in Ontario, the automobile concerns were getting trains of cars in which to ship their output. Automobiles, a mere luxury, could be shipped, but necessaries could not.
The Minister of Finance has stated that we on'this side are obstructive, that we are merely critical. I myself proposed that the duty on tractors should be removed, but that motion was voted down by the Government. The hon. minister cannot pretend that that would not have been an assistance to greater production in Canada.
We have the Provincial Government using them and we have enterprising farmers doing the same thing for the purpose of working more land and producing better crops. When we have a matter which is really vital, which is important, which is in the interest of greater production, and when we have a proposal of that kind made from this side of the House and every man on this side of the House votes for it, we have the Minister of Finance, who leads the Government, standing up and calling on every man at his side to vote it down. The same thing applies to the removal of the duty on seed -beans with regard to which we expect an answer from the Minister of Finance in the near future. Petitions signed by nearly every member of the council of Kent, signed by the warden and leading farmers throughout the county, have been sent to the Minister of Finance. Every section of that part of the country is anxious for it. The farmers are stalled. The unfavourable condition of the weather at the present time means that whoever puts in a crop will have to put it in later in the season than usual and that it will have to be either beans or corn because it will be too late for the farmer to put in oats and barley. It will not be surprising if we find that the same fate meets the resolution embodying that request. Yet we have the statement of the minister to-day that we are not trying to give the Government assistance by suggesting something which might be practical and in the best interests of the country.
I am glad to be able to say a few words on behalf of the resolution which has been introduced by my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) because I feel satisfied it is not any too soon that a resolution of this kind should be introduced or that some steps should be taken to assist the consumers if at all possible by the Government to at least get food supplies at prices

in keeping with the wages that labouring men are able to earn in the factory.
