speechtext:
I am not quite sure, Mr. Speaker, whether the fact that I have risen in ordeT to say a few words on this question is the occasion of your caution. I generally try to stick fairly closely to the text I undertake to speak upon, but 1 feel that it is a little unfortunate to be confined simply to the question fit flour when every hon. gentleman who has spoken has covered a rather wide field. However, I have a very few remarks to make and I shall endeavour as far as possible to stick to the subject at issue. As far back as March 1, 1915, I introduced to this House the following resolution :
That, in the opinion of this House, the circumstances arising out of the present war are such as to justify the Government of Canada in exercising supreme control over the quantity and destiny of our food exports, thereby regulating the prices at which bread, meat and other food products shall be sold1 for home consumption, while at the same time directing that our surplus food exports should only reach British or friendly countries.
It is upwards of two years since I introduced that resolution, and in January last, in further discussing the subject during the present session, I again drew attention to this proposition of mine submitted as an humble member of this House, for the regulation ,of prices and the control of food products.
I think the resolution brought forward by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) is a veTy fitting one and coming as
I do from a constituency composed pf 25,000 city residents and 8,000 or 10,000 residents in the country, I have to sail fairly close to the wind in order to satisfy both interests and not to offend either. However, I feel it is my duty as a public man not to be afraid to express the opinoin which I hold and have held strongly for the past two yeaTS, which is that the country being at war cannot be expected to live up to the .ordinary regulations which are sufli-cient in times of peace. In order that I may be fully understood, I do not think I can do better than to cite from Hansard what I said on the subject two sessions ago:
I said: The resolution standing in my name is one which I deem of great importance at the present time. It has no political significance, so far as I am concerned. It has appeared to me that for some months past it was the duty of those in charge of the Government of the country to keep a very good eye upon the food supply of the Dominion of Canada, and also to assist in every way possible the Mother Country in the tremendous struggle in which she is now engaged. I am aware that the principle contained in the resolution upsets to a certain extent what has been deemed proper economic law, that is, that the law of supply and demand regulates the prices of all commodities.
At the same time this war has upset a great many business axioms, has upset the calculations of many political economists and has brought to our attention the fact that a worldwide war is not dealt with by ordinary means nor controlled by ordinary circumstances. Supply and demand as a rule is a safe criterion for the fixing of prices of commodities. As far as I have been able to judge, Canada is the only country at present at war that has not given more or less consideration to this very important question. Very early in the war the Government of the sister Dominion of Australia, that great Commonwealth, which is also a large i producer of food, took possession of all supplies of wheat and arbitrarily fixed the price at $1.25 per bushel. That was done in one of the leanest years that Australia has seen in a long time. Their wheat crop was comparatively a failure. The supplies for home consumption were away below the requirements of that great country. New Zealand is in very much the same position and has been obliged to appeal to Canada for its supplies.
It is only consistent on my part that I should now again advocate the principle of the motion which I placed on the Order Paper then. The 7,000 workmen of the city of Brantford look upon this as the leading question of all the questions that are before this House or the country .at the present time. 'We are not asking this Government, nor are we asking this House, to dp anything that has not been already done by every one of the warring countries ex-

cept Canada. We take up the paper tonight -and in regard to the United 'States which has only ibeen about a month in the war we read in the Evening Journal this despatch from New York:
United Press Despatch.
New York, May 3.

"Submarine destruction has been steadily increasing for six weeks. The situation is one of extreme gravity, make sure of that."
With this warning Herbert C. Hoover, who is to be America's food dictator, arrived to-day from Britain. He left immediately for Washington.
Declaring that deaths in the industrial districts of Belgium had been "multiplied by three" on account of submarine operations during March and April, Hoover said the U-boats were the one big menace which must be eliminated in order to win the war.
"The European food situation as well as the general food situation there requires every possible effort we can make,'' he said. "What Europe needs most is wheat and what it must have is wheat, but it must also have beef and pork products. As for Belgium, the relief system is struggling to its feet after having been practically knocked out by the submarines. Five of our ships have been lost since March 1."
This further statement from one of our agricultural authorities, Mr. W. J. Black, appears in the same paper:
All over Canada the situation is grave. The prospects are far from bright, and the people may as well know it now. The seeding has been lamentably delayed by the weather this spring, and in the western states even less land is ploughed than has been heretofore the case. In Saskatchewan alone there were 1,500,000 acres less land ploughed last fall than the year previous.
This was due to the fact that the harvest was taken off the fields so late there was not time to get the land ploughed- before winter set in.
I think those quotations prove conclusively that we are at an acute crisis in the food situation. I have no political axe to grind and no particular desire to please either the farmer or the workingman beyond that desire which every citizen should have, to help -humanity whereever he can help it. I speak on behalf of the -workingmen of Canada, and especially of those who reside in my native city of Brantford, and I feel it is my duty to impress on the House the desirability of more control of food supplies. That applies not alone to flour but to all otheT food products. The day is near at hand when we must have a food dictator in Canada. I think we might with advantage have had one long ago. I do not mean by a food dictator a tyrant, a despot, or a czar, but one who
[Mr. Cockshutt.I
would make kindly suggestions to the people, appeal to them in the way of humanity, and ask them if they are not willing in time of war to sacrifice a little. It is all very well for you, someone may say to me, living at a first-class hotel, to propound a proposition like this. I should be only too glad if the -Government would tell the hotel keepers of this city and of all Canada that khey (must limit their menus to the barest fare, as they -have done in Great Britain, in France and in practically all European countries. Why should we be served with twice as much on our plates as any reasonable man should eat? Often it would be much better foT a man's stomach if he did not eat so much, but he iinust eat it all or waste it, and in my judgment the time for waste has passed. If this war continues-, we shall need a food dictator or a man who will come to us with propositions with regard to flour, meat, potatoes and1 all those necessities of life, and tell us that we should -not have more of them than is good for us, and should save all the food we can on behalf of those not so fortunately situated as we are. It may be said that the workingman has hi-s increased wages. So he has. But I want to tell you, as one who represents a working class community, that the wages have not advanced in nearly the same proportion as have the prices of foods. That is in the knowledge of every man who gives the slightest thought to it. We know that food prices have increased enormously. Wheat, which was 80 cents to 90 cents before the war, is $3 to-day. Flour, which sold at about $3 to $3.50 per hundred weight, is now $6 or $7 per hundred pounds. And the increase .does not apply to food only. Take coal, woollen goods, almost any textile goods and the same thing applies all through. And what has the workman got? He has got a very small wage increase over what he was obtaining before the war to pay for all these advances that have been placed upon the necessities of life.
May I make a few suggestions that I think, if followed up, would be of advantage. I have always appealed to the farmer in the same way as to the workingman. I am not saying anything here that I would not say before an audience of farmers or workingmen, and if I cannot be re-elected in my constituency I am quite willing to stay at home. I want to speak what I believe to be right and true and I declare that, in war times such as these, to say

that the law of supply and demand must continue to regulate the prices of all articles of commerce is to my mind to beg the question. I say that it wants something more drastic and these kid gloved methods that have been in vogue for so long will not do if this war continues. I say that with regard to recruiting as well as with regard to the food supply. We want to wake up and give a lead to the people of Canada, who, I believe are ready for a lead right now. They want somebody to suggest something practical that they can do to help the situation. They are anxious to have suggestions made as to ways in which they can assist, and if they can assist by cutting down the cost of living, I am sure that they will be ready to do so. Where is there a man who, knowing the suffering that exists to-day in Belgium, in Serbia, in Poland, in almost all the countries of Europe, where is there a man who is going to spend $3 o* $4 on a high-class dinner, and leave two-thirds of it on his plate, when he knows that his brethren of almost all the civilized nations of the earth are dying day by day for the necessaries of life? We say here every day, give us this day our daily bread. How many of us are thinking of the other chap who is not getting his daily bread? How many of us are ready to surrender any of the things that we have been squandering on ourselves in war times? When I read that lecture I apply it to myself as well as to anyone else. I know that I have spent money that I should not have spent. I know that I have not given as much as I should. I have tried to give and to do, but I know that I have not done half of what I should, and I know that if every member in his heart will only examine his ability to sacrifice and to do for others he will find that he, too, could do more.
We have before us to-day a proposition with regard to flour, but it applies to almost every article of food that goes on the workingman's table, and I say we have to remember those who work behind the benches as well as those who till the soil. I am not here to speak on behalf of one or the other, but to say a word for the honest working men of Canada. According to the census of 1911 there were 900,000 workers besides those on the farm who were dependent upon their daily wages for their daily bread, and while you may say that the farmer's lot is the hardest, I have tried a little of the farmer's life and a little of the workingman's, not a great deal of either, and I declare that the workingmen of the Dominion of Canada to-day put as much honest
labour on their daily task as any other class of the community, and that is not said with any disrespect to anybody. They have to work winter and summer, day in and day out, from seven in the morning until six at night, with one hour off, with a taskmaster often over them to see that they are on the job, and if they are two or five minutes late they are docked for it. That is the way the workingman of this country has to put in his time; he has a watch-clock on the job and has to be there on the moment and he must not knock off a moment before the time is up.
Now, what about these workingmen? Are they exercised about the prices of food? I think they are. I say they are very much exercised about the prices of food, and I believe that in the very near future this Government, or some other Government, must take in hand the prices of foodstuffs in the Dominion of Canada. I say that believing it to be true. It has been done in all other countries, and it can, and, I think, will have to be done here if this war continues. It is a practical necessity of the situation, absolutely. We have been living in a kind of fool s paradise here, it appears to me, for quite a while. We think we are m the war, but, barring the men we have sent across and the occasional thoughts we give to the caisuklty lists, I fear our efforts on behalf of the war are mighty small, our self-denial mighty little, and, I think, it is time that we all realized that the sufferings of humanity are our sufferings, and that we must bear our share of this white man's burden in the way a white man should.
These prices, which can be and ultimately must be controlled, can be controlled in ten minutes under the operation of some such resolution as I have proposed. There is no doubt about that; prices have been controlled in every other country in the world, and they can be controlled here. The United States, only a month at war, is talking of controlling prices immediately; why not Canada? Great Britain has done it, Australia, and India have done it, France has done it, Germany and Austria have done it. Belgium, Poland, and Serbia, unfortunately, have not any food to control, but every other war country that professes to have a Government at the head of affairs is controlling its food to-day and securing a fair distribution of it among the people. That is one of the duties of a Government; if necessary, we should even be put on rations. Owing to the high cost of living,
I think that that is a practical suggestion.

speechtext:
That is exactly what we have here; it is plainly set forth in the resolution. I say that the control of exports will result in the control of the price of food, immediately and absolutely-and not only food, but manufactured articles as well, if you wish. I do not want to be left out of this; let nobody make a mistake about that. I am prepared to submit to the very same regulation that 1 ask every citizen in Canada to submit to. I do not propose any class legislation, but I say that the control of all food exports would provide that after a certain maximum price has been reached-fix it where you will, but fix it where it is fair and just-no more goods shall go out until the price goes down. That will fix it, and fix it quickly. We may beat about the bush; we may have investigations; we may curse the middleman and every one who deals in food and every individual citizen who is not our own self; we may say that the other fellow is responsible, but when it comes to the final analysis the responsibility lies at the door of every citizen. We all have to do our share; we all have to give; we all 'have to practise self-denial, if need be, in order that all may live.
The workingmen have suffered much on account of the high cost of living. I do not say that there is any acute suffering at present, but they have been obliged to deny themselves many things that they would like to have upon their tables and that we, perhaps, have upon our tables. Their wages cannot pay for these luxuries that others are, perhaps, provided with. You say that the farmer will cease to produce if you begin to limit his prices. I do not think that that will happen. I am sympathetic with the farmer. In my own county I have many farmer friends of a lifetime whom I esteem as highly as I do any class in the community. I know that they are rational; I know that they are human. I know that if a woman or child knocks at the door of a farm house in the county of Brant or any other county in the province of Ontario, the farmer or the farmer's wife will say: you shall not go hungry from this door. It is the instinct of humanity to help the suffering. If in ordinary times $1.50 or $2 is a fair price for wheat; if $1.50 or $2 is a fair price for a bag of potatoes, 35 or 40 cents a fair price for a pound of butter and 25 cents for a pound of cheese,

it is no hardship on this or any other Government to say that owing to the exigencies of war, those prices should not be exceeded. Britain has a food dictator. He has not gone about with a big stick, but he has made suggestions with a view to the limitation of the cost of all the necessities of -life. Every hotel and restaurant in the great cities of Great Britain have a menu beyond which they cannot go. They are obliged to serve so many ounces of bread, so many ounces of meat, so much potato, and so on, and their meals are confined to two or three courses, according to the necessities of the case. We are asked to deal with a question such as this. I hear an hon. gentleman say:	"How would he reduce ploughs,"
if I am not mistaken. I am quite ready for my hon. friend to fix ploughs at his own price. The day has gone by when I can be held up with a threat about ploughs. I have explained in this House time and again that I have had absolutely nothing to do with the manufacture or control of ploughs for twenty years and if anybody in this House thinks that he can hold me up by shaking a big stick over me and talking about ploughs, I would like him to get up and try it. I have had that shot at me from both sides of the House and I tell you that it does not count with me worth a cent. I did not think that my hon. friend should have whispered that quite so loudly. The suggestion of ploughs is supposed to answer all arguments, and it has been made to me whenever I have attempted to say anything about the necessities of life. It has nothing to do with the question so far as I am discussing it, and, besides, I am propounding nothing now, as I have already said, that I am not prepared to submit to myself. I am trying to make valuable suggestions that will help to secure the control of food prices, and I am doing it in a serious way, because I think that is absolutely necessary.
It gives me a good deal of pain to have to dissent from my fellow-members. I would not do it unless a strong sense of duty led me to the conclusion that, representing a constituency such as I do, in a time of war such as this, as a citizen of Canada I should say what I think upon this great question. The time is near at hand, if this war continues, when some such suggestions as I have made will have to be put into operation. And if they are put into operation as I have suggested them, I guarantee that they will be effectual. What every other country has done

Canada can do. We want something of the heroism in onr acts at home that will, even if only in a very feeble way, compare with the acts of onr heroic sons across the water. If our heroism at home was half or quarter as great as that of our dear boys over the water, we would not have to speak as we do on this occasion. We should be ready to make sacrifices; we should be ready to deny ourselves in time of war. The ordinary influences of supply and demand are set aside by the unusual conditions. In the face of a world-wide war, millions of tons of food have gone to the bottom of the seas and we shall be months or years overtaking the loss that is being occasioned by the submarines. If in the face of these conditions we continue our wasteful methods, a sudden call of halt will come to us, the food supply will be gone and we will have only ourselves to blame, simply because we have thrown away the lavish gifts of nature that are scattered broadcast over the Dominion. I trust that the resolution that my hon. friend has introduced will be the means of causing the powers that be to think seriously about the regulation and control of all food prices and of all the necessities of our daily life, and particularly of the life of the workingman. That is a practical suggestion; it is one that will come in the near future; and in all kindness, but with full sincerity, I make these suggestions from one of the back benches, and I trust that my remarks will not be thrown away but that in the early future, we shall have, if not a dictator, some one who will come out with a lead and ask the people of Canada to live and let live, to sacrifice and to give, to help those who are in need, and to try to lighten the white man's burden, as represented by the workingmen of this country, for whom I say we cannot appeal too strongly. They are worthy of the utmost sacrifice on the part of every one of us, and we should endeavour to lighten their load which, I am sure, they find very onerous at the present time. Let the heroism shown by our boys at the front be shown in some measure by those of us who remain at home, and all these questions will be duly solved.

Mr. Speaker, I think the Government are, to a large extent, responsible for the high price of flour and the high cost of living in general. They are having a large amount of munition work done in this country and they are paying such prices to the manufacturers of munitions that the latter are making immense profits and are paying very high wages to their employees. I can understand that, at the start, it was necessary to pay extreme prices for munitions in order to get the business started, because the manufacturers were not equipped for making munitions and were unwilling to engage in a new business unless there was good remuneration in sight for them; but once the business was started and once the munition manufacturers throughout the country were clamouring for business, the Government should have adopted a little more business-like method and should have said to the manufacturers, when they wanted one or two million shells: Give us a bid; how many can you make, and at what price? Instead of doing that, the Government have fixed a price for munitions so high that the manufacturers have made huge profits and have been able to pay their employees-not all skilled labourers, but some of them men who were common day labourers-ten dollars, fifteen dollars and even more than that a day. The call to arms has come to every man in this country, the farmer as well as every one else, is supposed to send his sons to the front, and they have gone. Consequently, the farmer must have some one to cultivate Ms farm and I ask: Where is he to get the help to do his chores from five o'clock in the morning until nine o'clock at night at ordinary wages, if a man can make ten to fifteen dollars a day in a shell factory? Had the Government adopted more reasonable and intelligent methods of dealing with this matter, they would not to-day have to ask the munition manufacturers to cough up 75 per cent of their profits, because they would not have made those profits and it therefore would not be necessary to ask the manufacturers to give them back. Unfortunately, all of the labouring men of this country are not in the shell business. Employers engaged in ordinary lines of manufacture cannot afford to pay excessive wages to their employees, although they are probably paying wages from thirty to forty per cent higher than they were a year ago, and as the cost of living has increased more than thirty or forty per cent, the man who is working for the ordinary employer is up against a hard proposition to support his family, whereas the man who is employed on government work and is making five or six times the wages of his less fortunate brother is not to be pitied. It is the Government,

however, wh.o are responsible for the high cost of living by having this 'Government work done at higher wages than the ordinary business man or farmer can afford to pay. It may be late in the day to remedy this matter, but it is said: " Better late than never." I understand the Minister of Finance made the statement this afternoon that the law of supply and demand was the governing factor. I wish he had thought so when he was dealing with the newsprint proposition. He did not appear to think of the law of supply and demand then because he fixed the price of newsprint at least at one per cent per pound less than it can be made for.
The high cost of living is going to be a serious problem for the man in the ordinary walk of life or working in the ordinary factories, and the farmer also is up against a very serious proposition. The farmer is asked to produce more. Most of his sons have gone to the front and he has to go into the labour market fpr help and he cannot get any. The Government ought to consider this question, even at this late hour, and see that the men working on Government orders are paid about the same wages as the men working in the .ordinary factories. If the Government do so, they will be going a long way towards remedying the cost of living.

Mr. Speaker, the course that the debate has taken this afternoon and evening must satisfy the Government that this question is one of the greatest importance, and that it is not, as the Minister of Finance has stated, a matter of party politics. The Minister of Finance is usually fair, but I think to-day he was absolutely unfair to the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) who introduced this resolution, and to other members on this side of the House who spoke on it, when he characterized it as being largely political. I am sure nobody in the House will accuse the hon. member fpr Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) of making a political speech, and I think he has shown to the Government and to the House that it is not a matter of politics but a matter of absolute necessity that something should be done if conditions are going to continue at all reasonable in this Canada of ours. I congratulate the hon. member for Brantford on having foreseen this two years ago, long before any of us on this side of the House or on the other side of the House saw it in the same light. What is our position in this country? Can-[Mr McCrea.]
ada is a food producing country, and today is overflowing with food. Why, then, should there be such high prices as are asked to-day? It is only a few days ago that the Minister of Agriculture told the House that we had a surplus of 1,500,000 bushels of potatoes over and above the food and seed requirements of this country. If that is the case, how comes it that the price of potatoes is $4 a bag? Who is to blame for it? My hon. friend the Minister of Finance says it is a question of supply and demand. I do not for one moment think it is the law of supply and demand that has raised prices up to their present level. I want to be absolutely fair; I do not want to blame the Government for more than they are responsible for, but it does seem to me that if the Government had used foresight or even common sense, we should not be in the position we are to-day. If it is the law of supply and demand that is forcing prices up, how is it that the juice of wheat at Liverpool has not gone up $1 a bushel in the last few days? Liverpool, as we all know, sets the price of wheat for the world, but there has been no such advance there in the past few days. What I blame this Government for is that they have simply let matters drift until they have got into their present position. It is only a short time ago that wheat was at a reasonable pric.p in this country. Within the last six weeks the Minister of Trade and Commerce had representatives of the farmers' organizations in the West come to Ottawa, and he wanted them to sell the whole western crop of No. 1 Northern delivered at Fort William at $1.20 a bushel.

hon. gentleman's statement. The Government reports show that, of the wheat in the West, twenty-one per cent is still in the farmers' hands. They have introduced a resolution that munition manufacturers shall not be allowed to make more than 3i per cent profit, and that the dealers in foodstuffs shall not be allowed to make more than 6 per cent profit. How does that compare with what has been going on in Canada, wheTe they have been making, not 6 per cent, but in some cases close to 600 per cent on some of food products? the manipulators and middlemen to so manipulate prices that the price of food is almost out of the reach of the average working man in Canada. The Government are to blame and are greatly to blame. It is time that they were waking up, and time that they were realizing the position that the country is in. It has been stated to-day, and I want to emphasize it, that we do not know exactly where we are in this war. With German submarines sinking vessels at the rate of fifty to sixty a week, as reported, and it is very probable we are not getting the worst of the reports, the condition- is most serious. I add my voice to the voice of my hon. friend from Brantford, and I call on the Government to take action at once along the line of appointing some man in charge of the food of the Dominion and see that the price is not put out of reach. If it has gone up $5 in the last week or two, what is to hinder them from putting it up another $5?
I would be afraid to contemplate the condition of the people of Canada with flour at $20 a barrel. In a country that has much more food than it oan use, with flour at $14.50 a barrel, potatoes at $4 a hag, and lots of other things not quite in proportion, but also very high, surely the Government will realize their position at last and come forward and do something in the interest of the people of Canada. If they do not- and I want to say this as moderately as I know how take some action the people will hold the Government responsible, and absolutely responsible, not for the total advance m the prices of foodstuffs, but for not taking any action to regulate prices. There is no question at all that the great big advance that has been made in the last few days is not due to supply and demand, but is nothing more or less than speculation and allowing these manipulators of food, for _ their own profit, to put prices away up in order that they may make millions. Every working man will have to pay his share of the millions of profits that are being made to-day out of the huge advances in the prices of wheat and flour and other foodstuffs throughout Canada.

However, I feel that I can with fair safety assume that the character of the discussion, at all events the character of the attack, has been throughout much of the same nature as that to which I have just listened from the hon. member for Assiniboia. If the level of the discussion prior to that had been such as would accord with the dignity of Parliament and the seriousness of this time, I could not believe that the hon. member for Assiniboia would allow himself to descend to the plane that he occupied for so long.
Now, we are asked, in the first place, to believe that there is "something" that should have been done. I have heard that word "something" so often, in these two speeches, and indeed during many years, as the peculiar name of what ought to be done, that I have begun to long to have that "something" defined. What is this miraculous, mysterious "something" that should have been done, or ought now to be done, or has not been done, and so on? The hon. member for Assiniboia says that we have lain back and done nothing. While dealers in food supplies have made millions, while other countries have done so much, and while things were in such an excellent condition the world over, all but here, it is said we have lain back and rested on our oars. We have all listened to very considerable in the way of general criticism of that sort, but we have heard very little in the way of comparison with other countries. About the last remark the hon. gentleman made was this, and it is a remark I have heard from him times without number: These middlemen, he says, and these people of a general character that he feels safe in attacking, are making millions piled upon millions, while in other countries they will not permit such thing at all. In good old England they never permit anything like that, he says, and they have a dictator to see that nothing of that kind takes place. What are the only figures available to compare all the millions that are being permitted to be made in this country and all the millions that are permitted to be made in other countries? Fortunately, we are in a position to make a comparison, that I do not claim is final, but that at all events is useful, on this very subject. We have now information as to the excess profits war tax, which I think has been very fully collected-collected with wonderful success for the first year, much beyond in amount the expectations of hon.

speechtext:
gentlemen on this side of the House, and far beyond the expressed expectations of hon. gentlemen on the other side. The collections for the first year of 25 per cent of the excess profits tax over 7 per cent on corporations in Canada gave $12,500,000, and are expected to reach $15,000,000 when all are in for the first year. For the second year it is expected that they will reach $20,000,000. Let us take that first year and compare it with the amounts got by Great Britain, and we will learn a lesson that will be very useful if we just let it sink down far enough. If 25 per cent of excess profits over 7 per cent amount to $15,000,000, the whole excess over 7 per cent will reach $60,000,000. That is for this country with a population of about 8,000,000. In Great Britain they collected for the same purpose 50 per cent of the profits in excess of what was for each business the average for three years prior to the war. Now our average for three years prior to the waT would be over 7 per cent. However, our total profits over 7 per cent were approximately $60,000,000.
In Great Britain they took their 50 per cent of what was over and above a higher amount than 7 per cent-namely, the average profit for three pre-war years.
In this way they collected £139,800,000, so that their total profits (excess over the average for three years before the war), would be twice that sum, or about £280,000,000. This is roughly $1,400,000,000, or 24 times the excess profits in this country. Their population is approximately five times ours. So that, man for man, in that country they had in the first year of the war excess profits in Great Britain of nearly five times the excess profits in Canada.
Before I pass to another phase of the discussion I want to make clear once more to the House-I know it long ago was clear to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) if he would do himself and the House the justice of stating it, instead of misstating it-the relations of the Government to the recent offer of the British Government to purchase the surplus export wheat of this country. The British Government have what they call a Wheat Commission, which deals through agents in this country and the United States with the necessary wheat purchases for themselves and their Allies. They are the purchasers for themselves and in the main their Allies the world over. It is they who want the wheat for this purpose, and not the Government of Canada. That Wheat Commission met the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster)
[Mr. Meighen. 1
when he was over in London, and they made a proposition to purchase the surplus wheat of this country, as they had made similar propositions to purchase the surplus of Australia, New Zealand and the other overseas dominions. At that time the United States was not our ally, but was a neutral nation. They had already consummated their negotiations with the other dominions and they made their offer to purchase our wheat on such a footing, having regard to 'the ocean rates between the other dominions and Great Britain and us and Great Britain, they controlling that, to a large extent, as would make our wheat cost in Great Britain what the wheat purchased in the other dominions would cost there. However, after some discussion, Sir George Foster was able to show them that it would he fair to pay a little more for the Canadian wheat, and consequently he was able to get them to raise the offer a little; but it was their offer from the beginning, throughout and to the end. They advanced certain reasons to him why, in their judgment, keeping in mind the higher interests of this war and of this Empire and doing justice at the same time, as they felt, to the farmers of Canada, that offer should be accepted. Having arrived in Canada, Sir George Foster felt it his duty-and the Government felt he was only pursuing his duty-to lay the subject before such organized body -in this country as best represented the producers. Consequently an invitation was sent to the Canadian Council of Agriculture to come to Ottawa and to discuss with the Minister of Trade and Commerce the offer that had so been made, and to ascertain whether or not they would recommend its acceptance on behalf of those whom they represented. That offer was made in that way, and the reasons adduced by the British Government through their wheat commission why in their judgment the offer should he accepted were passed on by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as it was his duty to do, to the representatives of agriculture in Canada. They refused to give an opinion. They went back and consulted their associations in a body, and then refused the offer and made a counter proposal. The counter proposal was as stated by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), and it was at once communicated to the British Wheat Commission, who did not act upon it. Now those are very plain facts. I am not bringing them forward in order to erect the Government of Canada

into any great position of credit. We simply did a simple and a plain duty. But on such simple elementary facts, why does an hon. member stand in this House and seek to attack this Government alleging as he does, that we tried to persuade the farmers of Canada to .sell at $1.30 and refused afterwards to pay $1.70 when, as a matter of fact, we as purchasers were never negotiating with the farmers of Canada at all? These men speaking for the producers of Canada refused the offer	made by
the British Wheat Commission and the British Wheat	Commission has	not
acted upon their counter proposition. So if any attack is to be made in this House, it is to be made on the British Government and the British Wheat Commission. But I do not stand in this House and attack them, nor do I stand in this House and praise them. They know the situation better than we do and in the light as they saw it they refused, or have not so far accepted the offer. There the matter stands.
One who has listened to the hon. member for Assiniboia for eight years in this House as I have, who had listened to his diatribes against the Government for their animosity to the farming community, who had listened also to his pleas for the poor workingman to be allowed to buy his flour cheaper by the removal of duty, would not have thought that, two weeks after the duty on flour was removed, the hon. member would stand in this House and attack the Government for doing nothing to bring down the price of the breakfast of the workingman. He wants a dictator too. He wants a dictator to dictate not what the farmer should get for his wheat, but what the workingman is to pay for his flour. Could humbug go farther? I do not know whether he wants the same kind of a dictator as we heard proposed by an hon. gentleman behind me, a dictator who' does not dictate. We were asked solemnly by an hon. gentleman behind me to appoint a dictator who would assume his duties and prosecute his duties by making " kindly suggestions" to the people of Canada. I want to say that we have just a little less than 7,000,000 of this kind of dictators already. We have " kindly suggestions " being made until we need an embargo on suggestions in this country. We welcome the man who will say specifically what can be done and help to do it. Suggestions, " kindly suggestions" -we have had them from the beginning of the war. Talk about giving a lead. There
68J
is not a man in this House who has not given a lead, if that is giving a lead. Most of us have spoken on platform after platform, gentlemen on the other side of the House as well as on this side; there is scarcely one who has not given that kind of a lead ever since the war began, asking that we exercise thrift, asking that we produce more, asking that we help the boys at the front and behave ourselves in Canada . something in the way that they have behaved themselves on the battle fields of Flanders. That is what thousands are doing. There has been leadership in abundance of that kind. We do not want a czar, we do not want anything in the way of an imperator, according to the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt). We want a dictator who will make something in the way of suggestions as to what may be done to keep down individual expenditure in Canada, and the waste of our food and our resources. Why, everybody knows what to do to keep down waste in this country-do not waste. Everybody in the country knows that already. It may be, and I am not going to say the time has not come or is not soon coming, when we will need to go further than make " kindly suggestions." It may be that the time will come when something will be done by way of compulsion. But if we are to have compulsion, let us call it by its proper name, and not endeavour to introduce it under all these dead phrases about doing " something," and all the rest of it. There is one step beyond the suggestion step, and that is compulsion, and if any one thinks we must have compulsion let him stand up like a man and say it, and not pursue these soft glove evasions all the time.
We have been listening to-night to much in the way of encomium of the United States. Well, I am not going to offer any criticism of the United States, of what they have done or of what they have failed to do, but I do not think the time has quite come for passing encomiums on a country, or deprecations of our own country by way of comparison, merely on the basis of the introduction of a Bill into the United States House of Representatives. We, too, have had a few Bills 1 " introduced " into this House. We had a few " resolutions " last night. For example, we had one resolution not only introduced, but actually going ,through-^or failing to go 'through-with the imprimatur on it of the Liberal party in Canada, which, if it had become law, would have taken out of the pockets of people who happened to have saved money

and had left it in the banks for Jive years, all the money that they had there, giving them not a dollar find no indemnity whatever in return. We have had all kinds of "resolutions" and " introductions," too. But it is time enough to pass encomiums and eulogies when the United States gets something done towards winning this war and towards prosecuting it the way we are prosecuting it. The other day a magazine in United States sent a message to Great Britain to Lord Northcliffe, perhaps the severest critic of British policy that has arisen since the war began, or that ever arose, and asked him if he had any suggestion to make to the United States as to how they could best address themselves to the duty of prosecuting the war. What was the suggestion that he sent? !He said: " If you enter the war, you will find that waging a great war under democracy is a new and vast experiment " 'If he had stood in this House of Commons and listened to this debate, he would surely have thought it was indeed a vast and perilous experiment. He said, further: " If you come in, I have one thing to say to you, and it is this: you can learn a great deal from the example of Canada." Those words are printed on the pages of Everybody's Magazine, where all the world can read them. Theodore Roosevelt wrote an article in a United States publication. He, perhaps, has been the severest critic of American policies since the war began. His name stands out in this country as unexcelled among his fellow-citizens. He said: "I am not an adherent of the principle of the voluntary system. But the voluntary system has achieved much, and Canada has shown to the world the utmost that can be done by the voluntary system." That is what the world's biggest men looking on Canada impartially from without thinks of what this country has achieved. Now if hon. gentlemen opposite want compulsion introduced in the military forces of this country or in the civil forces in the matter of fo.od dictatorships and prices, let them say specifically that they will back up compulsion and they will gain their wishes at least much faster than they will by this infinite amount of aimless and pointless talk.

Mr. Speaker, I always listen, with
interest to the very eloquent speeches of the Solicitor General. He has made a reputation for himself of steering away from the real subject at issue, and I can assure him [Mr. Meighen.J
that in the art of keeping away from the subject and of not touching the issue at all he never did himself better justice than he has done on this occasion. It is sad to watch the tactics of the generals of the Government and the dope which they deal out to their followers around them when a question of this kind is brought up. The first thing they do is to get their supporters gopd and mad against the Opposition so that they will take a plunge into anything and vote for the Government whatever the question may be. That dope has been meted out by the Solicitor General and it has been dosed all over the members on the other side by the great leader of doping, the Minister of Finance. Hon. gentlemen,
I think, have been sufficiently doped and dosed by this time to accept almost anything that may be submitted to them. But the hon. generals of the 'Government on that side of the House must not forget that the electors of Canada, supporters of hon. gentlemen opposite, the men who sent them here, are not partaking of this dope which the 'Solicitor General is spraying around. Sitting in their houses or going about their business, they have opportunity of deliberately considering the question from a proper point of view and outside the baneful influence of this dope that is being cast around.
I think that the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. G. W. Kyte) is entitled to much credit and commendation from both sides of the House for bringing before the House the very important matter that he drew to our attention this afternoon. If the discussion had been participated in only by members on this side of the House, it might be said that the subject was a partisan one and had in it no value or virtue besides that of partisanship. But we find the Minister of Finance, who is leading the Government, the Minister of Labour and the Solicitor General, and such able and eloquent men as the member for Brantford (Mr. W. F. Cockshutt) taking part in this discussion; therefore we feel that it must be a question of grave import and should be dealt with in that spirit.
I must apologize to the Solicitor General on behalf of some of us on this side who suggested that the Government might be doing something. The member for Assini-boia (Mr. J. G. Turriff) suggested that the Government might have taken steps to procure a large quantity of wheat at a certain price subject to their control in order to meet present necessities. The hon. Solicitor General said that the Government would

not do such a thing; he became indignant at the idea that the Government should be doing anything on behalf of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, and who may not have an opportunity of speaking again. I must apologize to every member of the Government for supposing for one moment that they would do anything of a practical character.
We are told that so far as the subject matter of the resolution is concerned we in Canada are in a better position than the people of other parts of the world. The hon. member for Richmond, in speaking the other night, made it plain from reliable facts and figures that cannot be controverted that the cost of living in this country has gone up 44i per cent, while in the Commonwealth of Australia-a sister dominion inhabited largely by the same class of people, having the same kind of industries, being more like Canada than any other part of the Empire-the cost of living has increased only 9J per cent. Does the Solicitor General think that our country compares favourably with our sister colony in the matter of the cost of living? I submit that it does not. The cost of living has been kept down to an increase of only 9} per cent in Australia by reason of governmental action, and there is no reason why the same governmental action should not take place in Canada and produce similar results.

speechtext:
There is no need of putting an extraordinary and absurd situation. If our soldiers in France were starving, we would divide our last bite with them. I would go on one meal a day and send the other' two meals to the soldiers in France; I would do anything to help them; but the situation is not pressing nor present, and we should deal with facts and circumstances and situations as they are, and not take impossible ones that are not yet in sight and ask how we should deal with those things. This Government refuses to deal with conditions that are impelling, conditions that cry for remedy, conditions that are in the acutest possible stage. Therefore what is the good of asking me to tell what should be done in an extraordinary condition which has not yet arisen? We are trying to stir the Government up to take some steps in regard to the situation as it is, and then after we get them agoing, perhaps they will do something if such an extraordinary circumstance as the hon. gentleman has mentioned should arise.

I wish, for a moment, to refer to the manner in which the motion of my hon. friend from Richmond was received by the Government. I always sympathize with a man who keeps within his limits and who does not try to fly beyond the atmosphere and heights to which God and Nature intended him to soar. I, for that reason, sympathize with my good, congenial friend the Minister of Labour when he quietly and complacently accepts the situation, knows that he did nothing and smiles when he is told of it. I am sure that he must have enjoyed and quietly laughed to himself at the comedy that he has put on this afternoon. He told us about the heaps of wheat and straw, and particularly chaff that there were in Russia. It is a great consolation to the child down in the county of Cape Breton, where I come from, who may be crying for bread, to be told that there is abundance of it in Austria, Russia and other places. What I want to deal with, what the resolution deals with and what we want to stir this Government on, is the actual question that is now before Parliament. The Minister of Labour was honest enough to say that he did nothing at all except, forsooth, to send a man down to Montreal. That mission to Montreal has about the same effect as if one's house in the city of Ottawa were "burning and the fire brigade arrived on the scene and they all stood back, and when a man would ask them: Why do you not put out the fire? they said, we have sent to Montreal for a bucket; when the bucket arrives from Montreal we will try to put out your fire. The one reason is just as effective as the other. Seven million people, we are told by the Solicitor General, are deeply interested in this question of the price of flour, and yet the only step the Government can take is to send a learned gentleman of my own profession to the city of Montreal to make -slight inquiries as to whether the price of flour has gone up or down. I cannot for the life of me see what possible effect that will have. I was speaking about the way in which this proposition was received, and I was delighted to find the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) speaking on this question, not as a new one, because he has given us largely the same views that he presented to this House two years ago. He cannot be accused of being favourable, from a partisan -standpoint, to any ideas we put forward on this side of the House. He has spoken more strongly than anyone on this side along the line of some action being 
taken by the Government. I think the hon. member for East Si-mcoe (Mr. W. H. Bennett) stated that this was all political buncombe. That is strong language, and I venture to say that he will not take the responsibility of telling the hon. member for Brantford that -he, as a good, strong, straightforward party man, always, a party man, came into this House this evening for the purpose of embarrassing this Government and talking political buncombe. Therefore, I think we must all reach the conclusion that the language used by the hon. member for East Simcoe was ill-advised and ill-considered, and that when in the -quiet of his chamber he will think over it and think of the great question that is at stake, he will revise his opinion, and that if he had to speak again he would not use that very strong language. He was, how-' ever, to some extent, justified in his attitude by the speech of the Minister of Finance, who was very irritable. I was just thinking to myself what was the most distressing circumstance that I could put him in from a physical standpoint, that would put him in the irritable position he was in, and I was thinking that if I could get a lobster dragging a Scotch thistle down his spine that would be about the -sensation mat would put him in the nasty position he was in. It would be well for a man in the high sphere that the minister is in not to appear as if the lobster and the Scotch thistle were going down his back when he deals with questions of this kind. When men take high and responsible positions they must know that with the position goes the responsibility of receiving criticism and sometimes criticism that will not be just. The hon. member for Richmond approached this question this afternoon in a most reasonable and rational frame of mind, and there was no justification for getting into this apparent fury into which the Minister of Finance worked himself unless it was for the sole and only purpose of spraying around this dope in order to get his men behind him into that frame of mind where their party spirit would be up and they would be determined to vote for him, regardless of every other consideration, because he represented the Government. I could understand the Government's reception of this subject to-day if it was a new question, but it is not a new thing for a Government to deal with matters of private concern in this country. It is not a new thing, for instance, for this Parliament to establish a railway commission, whose duty it is to deal with private business, to-

regulate prices, not the price of food, but prices of commodities in this country are nevertheless regulated to some degree by the rulings of that commission. I venture to say that every province in this Dominion has its utilities board. In the province of Nova Scotia we have one, and I think there is also one in New Brunswick, and I am pretty sure there is one in Ontario, and in the other provinces of the Dominion. There are some cities and towns in this Dominion that do not own their own water supply; in some cases it is owned by corporations, and if the water supply is not properly furnished or if too much is being charged for it, the utilities commission of the province has the right to regulate the supply and control the price of the water. In like manner the price of lighting, telephones, and other public utilities are subject by legislation to the control of independent men appointed by the Government. The principle is therefore admitted. This Government not only admits the principle, but they have acted upon it in regulating the price of news print. Having acted upon the principle, having thus put themselves in the position of dealing with cases of this kind because too high prices are said to he charged, why do they not deal with flour or wheat or any other commodity just as readily as they deal with the raw material that goes into the making of a newspaper? I submit that a newspaper, while an excellent thing to have, is a luxury to a great many people, and we can do without luxuries. We can do without newspapers, although perhaps life may be very dull without them, but it is much more important that a workingman should be able to buy butter, bread and cheese for his wife and family than that he should open up the newspaper to them. The Minister acted quite properly, I presume, in helping out the newspaper people, but he gets into a passion and says that we are unrighteously and unfairly attacking the citadel of the Government when we suggest to him that the price of flour and other foodstuffs in the country should be brought down to that level where the purchasing power of the poor man could buy them. The principle, therefore, has been adopted in local politics, and has been acted upon by this Government. For that reason the Government have no ground for looking upon this as a new thing, or for taking umbrage at myself or the hon. member for Richmond or any other member who has spoken in support of the idea presented in this motion.
The Minister of Finance pointed out to us this afternoon that we have 100,000,000 bushels of wheat in this country. If there is any country in the world where flour should be cheap, that country is Canada. Canada, the United States, the Argentine Republic and other countries producing wheal in large quantities-these are the countries in which flour should be cheap. I cannot conceive of any good reason why the Government will permit the
10 p.m. price of flour to soar beyond what is reasonable. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) told us that a fair price to the farmer, and one that he was willing to accept, was $1.70 a bushel. This is a fair basis to start with, and if the Government can secure to the people of Canada wheat at $1.70 a bushel, what justification is there for them allowing it to go up to something like $3 a bushel as it is now. I submit to the minister and to the Government that if it is true that flour i3 selling in the neighbourhood of $13 a barrel here, the miner at Glace Bay or Sydney will be paying at least $16 a barrel. My hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) says it was selling down there at $15 a barrel last week. Since then the price has gone up $1.20 a barrel, so the miner down there must be paying $16 or more. I should like to point out to the minister that a miner with a family of seven or eight children would consume about two barrels of flour a month. A barrel of flour does not last in a house of that size more than two weeks, perhaps not that long. I venture to say that the earnings of the miner are not more than $48 or $50 a month. When you take $32 out of that for two barrels of flour, it leaves him only $16 to pay his rent and buy coal, groceries, clothing and so forth for his family. With flour at this price he cannot live at all, and the hon. member for Richmond and all of us come here and plead in the only place where we can seek for a remedy for this condition. The Government might well find fault if we had any other way open to us of trying to cut down the price. They might well say then, "Leave us alone, we are running the war; go somewhere else for a remedy." But we have no other place to go, and that being so, we are justified in coming here to the only power that can deal with questions of this kind.
According to the Minister of Finance we have 100,000,000 bushels of wheat in this country. That means 22,222,222 barrels of flour, allowing, as the minister said, four and one-half bushels of wheat to the bar-

rel. I presume we have in this country about 100,000,000 barrels of flour, besides the wheat that is not ground. That is an enormous quantity of flour, more than we could expect to consume in this country for some time. But supposing we had nothing in the shape of ground flour in this country to-day, this 100,000,000 bushels of wheat that the Finance Minister speaks of would mean three and one-quarter barrels of flour to every man, woman and child in this country, and we are told we must pay something like $16 a barrel for every barrel of this flour. Surely there is no necessity for one moment for us to pay such an ex-'hofbitant price, and we come to the Minister of Finance and ask him to take this matter in hand. These speculators occupy the front seats in the commercial synagogues and temples of this country. I submit to the minister that they pollute and contaminate the blessed streams of fair and righteous merchandising, and we are now asking the Minister of Finance, the Zac-dheus of the Government, to take the knotted cords in his strong right arm and drive from the temples and synagogues, as was done of old, these men who are polluting the temple and contaminating the trade of this country. He may not have any precedent in his Government for this, but if he will look to sacred history he will find the One of old took the cords and drove those rascals out of the temple that were trying to rob and destroy the people and contaminate the trade of the country. We appeal to the Minister of Finance now to do the same thing to those men who are polluting our trade, and I am sure he will have the people of Canada behind him.
Of course, it may be a new departure for the Government to do something; but I would remind the hon. minister that before they came into office the people were accustomed to a Government that did things and saw to it that the people were protected. And if those now in power wish to gain the confidence of the people in the same degree that their predecessors did, they must come down, as Zaccheus of old came down from the tree, and do something to remedy public grievances. This Subject is one of such vast importance to the people that I, representing here, as I do, a large body of working men, even though I could not bring anything new to the discussion I deemed it my duty to make myself heard in support of this motion. It has been said that we are attacking the farmers, and we are told that this is the day of the farmer. We 
are not attacking anybody, and I submit that this is not anybody's day to make undue profits. The dire distress of the country in this awful war is not anybody's opportunity to make undue profit or charge exorbitant prices. Every one of us owes a great deal to his profession or line in life, but none of us must take advantage of present circumstances to profit unduly by what we produce. The lawyer, or the doctor, has no business to charge more because there is a war, and the farmer owes a duty to the public to which he looks for the purchase of his goods. No man should take advantage of the fact that the war is on to demand prices that he could not possibly get at other times.
I trust the Minister of Finance and his colleagues will consider this matter carefully, and above all that they will disabuse their minds of the idea that there is any polities in the motion under discussion. Speaking for myself, nothing could be further from my mind. Nor do I see how political capital could be made out of this matter. It is our simple duty to the people to make Canada a good country to live in;, and if prices of foodstuffs are soaring, making it impossible for men with small wages to enjoy reasonable conditions of life, it is the duty of this Government to try to remedy that evil, and it is my duty as a member of the House to point out what seems to me the way in which the Government can be of service to the people.

speechtext:
The times in which we are living are such as we have never before experienced. The liberty of the nation and of the individual is at stake. We are asked by the resolution now before the House to adopt very radical measures indeed with regard to one of the staple articles of food, and we have heard a good deal of criticism from hon. gentlemen opposite of the lack of action on the part of the Government with regard to this and other questions. I know that the tendency under ordinary conditions is to seek to make as much political capital as possible out of any question that comes up in Parliament. But at such a time as this I believe anything of that nature should be foreign to our minds, but that we should look on these questions honestly, and wholly in the interest of the country and of the cause for which we are contending. The slogan for the last few months has 'been " greater production." We have heard from practically every urban centre in Ontario, and we might almost say throughout

the whole Dominion-men and women, everybody, urging upon the farmers the need of greater production in view of the danger confronting the people of the whole world. I 'believe it is wise that this should be done. The danger thus far is only one that is apprehended, but it may become a very real danger indeed. But I do not believe that the present situation has come about altogether as a result of this war. I believe we were leading up to this condition for a number of years before the war. There was an exodus from the rural districts to the urban centres for many years prior to 1914. I have viewed that movement with a good deal of concern, and have satisfied myself-and have so expressed myself on many occasions within the last fifteen years -that the time would come when the folly of the course pursued would become apparent to the people. It is unfortunate that a critical period should intervene at a time when we are called upon to put forth every exertion in the struggle in which we are engaged. I view with a good deal of concern the statement in the press that flour advanced by $1.20 ra barrel yesterday. The strtement has been made by a number of hon. gentlemen opposite that we should commandeer the wheat in the hands of present owners. The Minister of Finance has told us that a good deal of that wheat is owned by the Government of Great Britain, and is to be made available for the men who are contending in the struggle at the front. We also know that if you wish to promote production of food you must not hamper, but must encourage those who are engaged in that work. The argument has been advanced by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) that the British Government, having made an offer of $1.30 a bushel for wheat, we should have appointed a dictator and should have purchased wheat at the same price. He suggested the price fixed by the Farmers' Association of Western Canada. I do not know that there is any other profession under the sun that is more of a gamble than farming. The farmer of Western Canada have no certainty -as to what the result of bis harvest is going to toe. Seeding has just started now in a great deal of Canada and as to what the result will be nobody can tell. It may be that a great injustice would have been done to many farmers in Canada if the price pf wheat had toeen fixed at even $1.70 a bushel because such a price is of very little use to the farmer if he has little to sell. It is the same in many of the older sections of Canada. You find that
people are continuously referring to the enormous profits that the farmers aTe making I know tenant farmers who have the greatest struggle pf their lives to make both ends meet. High prices are absolutely useless to the farrnef if he has nothing to sell and he has much to purchase. That is the very condition that is confronting a great many people to-day. To commandeer the wheat crop of Canada is a very serious matter but it has been glibly suggested by a number of speakers that it should be done with regard to wheat and a great many other commodities as well. Potatoes have been referred to as another commodity which the Government should take control of. It is a remarkable thing that this scarcity of certain products has practically taken place in almost all parts of the world at the same time. It is something unique in the experience of the world that a shortage such as we experienced last year in the potato crop should have been so general in other countries. The same thing applies to wheat. With a thousand million bushels of wheat short last year, is it any wonder that the price of wheat has risen? Yet some hon. gentleman opposite say that the law of supply and demand should have nothing to do with this. Why should it not have anything to do with it? What other law should apply but the law of supply and demand? I believe that is the law that is regulating prices to-day. I believe the prices that -are being fixed in the great markets of the world are a result of this condition. I wish that the law pf -supply and demand was the only law in fixing all prices. One of the reasons given for the high cost of living has been the large wages paid to the workmen engaged in the manufacture of munitions. I do not think that has had so much to do with it as spine other things. This is a condition that has not arisen since the war but it is one up to which we have toeen gradually approaching for many years past. In Ontario, during the last twenty years, 125,000 people who were producers have moved to the towns and cities or to some of the other provinces. If this condition is general throughout the country what else could you expect but a food shortage? That is the very thing that we are confronted with to-day and the fixing of prices is not going to increase the quantity of foodstuffs but production will be increased only by the people who will get out and work on the land. Then, let the law of supply and demand govern. We have reached a stage to-day

where agriculture is coming into its own. its own.
We have a country extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific, almost 4,000 miles, in extent one of the grandest stretches of agricultural land in the world, and instead of finding about fifty per cent of the people living in cities and towns, we should find a larger proportion out cultivating these broad acres and endeavouring to do something to meet the conditions with which we are confronted to-day. It is all very well to get up here, on the very next day aftei this unusual increase in the cost of wheat and flour, and advance the arguments that have been advanced. It would have been much better if we had realized that we have been approaching these conditions for a number of years past. I believe one of the chief reasons for the condition that confronts us to-day is the organization that has taken place in almost all other classes except those engaged in agriculture. The labour unions, we know, have organized themselves and the pay of the wage earner has been increased. I do not say it has been unduly increased hut it has been increased to such an extent that the farmer has been unable to pay the price being paid by the manufacturers; consequently the labourers have drifted into the towns and cities and that is one of the things that has brought about the present scarcity. But it does not apply to Canada only. It is general'throughout the whole world. In the United States, in the early days of the war, it was necessary to pass a war tax. Conditions became as acute there as in Canada. The removal of the dirty on wheat and flour by the Government a few days ago, I believe, was a wise measure. It was something I was opposed to in years gone by hut under the *abnormal conditions- with which we are now faced I think it was a wise measure on the part of the Government. I could not help thinking, as I listened to the hon. member for Assiniboia and other members opposite who have been condemning the Government to-night, what an outcry they would have raised if the Government had not taken the action they did in regard to this question.
. I do not intend to say anything more in regard to that but I do feel that we must not lose sight of the fact that the people who have been endeavouring to keep the flag flying on the farms of Canada are entitled to some consideration at this time and that the future welfare of the country 
is bound up in these men who have been working long hours, who have been struggling under a mighty and heavy handicap in order to keep themselves going. We have practically reached the breaking point hut I do not think for one moment that it is possible for the Government nor should we expect them to rescue us from the results of our own action. It will take time and the men of this country and .other countries must realize that they have to till the soil in order to get food products. *You cannot live on manufactured articles but you must live as a result of the fruits of the soil. No one regrets the suffering, which undoubtedly is in existence to-day in many places as a result of the high cost of living, more than the farmers of this country. I say further that the farmers have done their best. There is no class of people in Canada, the United States, or, I believe, any other country, that have laboured more diligently and with less reward ,for their services than have those who have been and are engaged in agriculture.
Mr. GEORGE W. KYTE (Richmond, N.S.): Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the very interesting debate we have had this afternoon justifies me for making the motion which I presented at the opening this afternoon. While we have not received any assurance from the Finance Minister, who spoke more particularly on behalf of the Government, that the very fair and reasonable request which I made will be taken seriously into his consideration, we have the satisfaction of knowing that the Liberal opposition does not stand alone in the desire to improve the conditions as outlined by me in this motion. We had a very interesting and illuminating address from the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt) this afternoon, and his address ought to be a complete and effective reply to the allegation made by the Finance Minister that we on this side are actuated by motives of partisanship in the resolution which is now before the House, and which has been debated. The Finance Minister endeavoured to argue that it would be quite impossible for the Government to take any such action as suggested by me, and that in face of the fact that similar action was taken on a very important commodity to which I referred in my opening observations. I have a little more fully looked into that question since I addressed the House this afternoon, and I desire to communicate that information to the House. The proposal to fix the price of news print that was made to the Min-

ister of Finance some weeks ago was accepted by him as a fair and reasonable proposition. What did he do? Officers of his department were sent to the manufacturers of pulp, and these officers proposed to the paper manufacturers that they must dispose of their paper at a price $10 in excess of that which they received a year ago. That price was not acceptable to the manufacturers of paper, and a subsequent offer was made by the officials of the Finance Department, which was to the effect that the manufacturers of paper must accept the sum of $2.50 per hundred pounds, or $50 a ton, for 20 per cent of the produce of their mills, which was estimated to be the quantity required for consumption in Canada. As to the balance of that production, they were free to sell it in whatever market they	could and	at whatever price
they could obtain. With regard to the	question of the price of flour
and wheat referred to in my resolution, my proposition is solely that we eliminate the influence of the stock speculators in increasing the price of these commodities to tne consumer. The total consumption . of wheat in Canada for many years has been about 50,000,000 bushels. It was pointed out by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) that the total population of Canada could not consume more than 25,000,000 bushels before the next crop is harvested and garnered. It is not then a matter of commandeering the whole wheat product of this country,, because we have in Canada, according to the statement of the Minister of Finance, 100,000,000 bushels of wheat. It resolves itself down to a question ito be disposed of in- a manner similar to the manner in which the Finance Minister disposed of the question of news print at the request of the newspaper publishers.
The Solicitor General asked many times: What is it that the members of the Opposition ask the Government to do? He reiterated time and again that the doing something was entirely too indefinite, and that it was up to the Opposition to make some concrete suggestion as to what ought to be done under the circumstances. He was not present during the debate when other hon. members on this side of the House addressed themselves to the subject, and so had no opportunity of knowing what suggestions came from this side of the House. For his benefit I would repeat once more what my suggestion has been. It is to take over all the wheat outside of that which is in the actual possession of the
farmers at present-and the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) is willing that even the wheat at present in possession of farmers should be taken over-that that wheat be controlled by the Government; that the Government should go to the millers and ask them to mill that wheat at a reasonable price and distribute it to the consumers in Canada. If the millers should be unwilling to do that, the Government should then take control of the mills, should themselves mill the wheat at a reasonable compensation to the millers, and distribute it to the consumers. That is a concrete proposition, and I think the suggestion of the Solicitor General that we have not offered any proposal looking towards the solution of the difficulty is not justified in the light of speeches from this side of the House. The Solicitor General, while sidestepping the real question under consideration, went into some figures to show that Great Britain obtained a very much larger amount of money out of its war taxes, relatively, than did the Dominion of Canada. I do not know why the Solicitor General offered that argument to the House except to show that the manufacturers in Great Britain were making very much larger profits, relatively, than the manufacturers in Canada. Of course, the Solicitor General did not point out to the House that the basis of taxation in England differs vastly from that which is applied in Canada at the present time. The Chancellor o'f the Exchequer, a few days ago, brought down his Budget proposals, which include taxation of war profits up to 80 per cent. The total taxation to be exacted by the Finance Minister in Canada under the new war taxes does not amount to more than 30 per cent at the veTy outside, so that if a larger proportion of taxation is derived from the taxation of war profits in England than in Canada it is due to the larger proportion which is exacted by the Government, and not to larger profits by the manufacturers.
